Daily social rejection was prevalent but typically low in intensity. When adolescents experienced more rejection than usual, they reported increased loneliness and irritation and decreased cheerfulness. These associations were stronger for offline than online rejection and were amplified when rejection occurred across both contexts. Importantly, maladaptive CER strengthened rejection-related loneliness, whereas stronger developmental increases in DLPFC activation across childhood attenuated adolescents’ loneliness responses to rejection. Our findings show that the emotional impact of everyday social rejection reflects individual differences in neurodevelopmental maturation and highlight emotion regulation as a potential mechanism underlying adolescents’ social sensitivity.

articles.title: Communicative Milestones: Modeling Age of Attainment in the First two Years
articles.authors: Miriam Teresa Löffler; Lisa Wagner; NA; Giancarlo Natalucci; Moritz M. Daum
articles.abstract: Early communicative milestones, such as first words and gestures, emerge within the broader context of overall child development. However, because studies typically focus on individual milestones and assess them cross-sectionally, they capture whether or not a milestone has already been achieved, but not when it first emerges — the Age of Attainment (AoA). To address this gap, we analyzed longitudinal data from 4,359 children collected through the Pebbles App, a smartphone-based developmental diary, in which respondents report whether and when a milestone was first observed. This approach provides fine-grained data and allows us to study the underlying dimensionality of the AoA of 14 early communicative milestones within the first two years of life. Exploratory factor analysis revealed a three-factor structure: (1) babbling (e.g., reduplicated babbling), (2) early nonverbal communication (e.g., pointing), and (3) linguistic productivity and gestures (e.g., producing first words). These factors were interrelated, which suggests that very early milestones (e.g., babbling) serve as markers that predict later communicative development within the first two years. The factor structure was invariant across different contextual groups (e.g., sex, caregiver education, or preterm status). Our results provide an important framework for understanding early communicative trajectories through AoA.

articles.title: Nature immersion in virtual reality does not reduce naturally occurring muscle pain or improve motor outputs during prescribed or self-regulated tasks
articles.authors: Callum O'Malley; David Harris; Sam William Hughes; Jack Cottrell; Dan Lloyd; Samuel James Vine; Tom Arthur
articles.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) can reduce experimental and clinical pain, yet it remains unclear whether these effects translate to naturally occurring muscle pain (NOMP) experienced during physical tasks. This study examined whether nature immersion presented through immersive VR attenuates NOMP and enhances motor performance during prescribed and self-regulated exercise. Two within-participant crossover studies were conducted. In Study 1, twelve healthy participants completed a stepped incremental cycling task to exhaustion under three conditions: immersive VR (nature scene), a two-dimensional sham display, and a no-intervention control. Pain onset, NOMP intensity, perceived effort, and time to exhaustion were measured. In Study 2, twenty-four participants performed intermittent isometric handgrip contractions at fixed light (13/100) or strong (50/100) perceived effort under the same conditions, with self-regulated force output and NOMP intensity measured. Immersive VR did not significantly delay pain onset, prolong time to exhaustion, reduce NOMP intensity, or lower perceived effort compared with sham or control conditions. A small reduction in NOMP intensity occurred early in the cycling task, but effects were trivial and not sustained. In Study 2, NOMP intensity, force production, and fatigue-related declines were similar across conditions. Exploratory analyses showed no moderating effects of sex, environmental presence, or fatigue. Overall, these findings demonstrate that nature-based VR immersion has limited effects on NOMP or motor performance. This likely reflects a mismatch between central mechanisms targeted by VR and strong peripheral drivers of NOMP. Consequently, VR hypoalgesia appears pain-type dependent and potentially pain-intensity dependent, with effects limited to lower pain intensities.

articles.title: The case of Michelle: Solutions of best sport psychology practice using four psychological perspectives
articles.authors: Emmanouil Georgiadis; Maurizio Bertollo; Sara Biondi; Cristiana Conti; Helen Davis; Thomas W. Gretton; Berit Kauffeldt; Efrosyni Mitsiou; Karin Moesch; Orestis Panoulas
articles.abstract:
Practitioners in sport psychology have long emphasized the importance of intervention plans informed by diverse philosophical and psychological perspectives. However, few publications present practical models drawn from various schools of thought. This paper addresses that gap by presenting responses developed within an international intervision group of sport psychology practitioners, who meet monthly to exchange best practices. We focus on the case of Michelle, a 16-year-old elite gymnast who sustained a serious injury requiring surgery and a prolonged recovery before returning to training and competition. To support Michelle’s rehabilitation, we outline four distinct intervention approaches: the Integrative Approach, the Mindfulness- and Acceptance-based Approach, the Psychodynamic Approach, and the Existential Approach. Each framework provides structured, theory-consistent methods and assessments tailored to the athlete’s physical and psychological needs during recovery. These approaches highlight distinct pathways to enhance resilience, foster motivation, and support reintegration into sport. We aim to inspire young practitioners to select approaches that align with their academic and clinical training, while also encouraging experienced professionals to expand their repertoires beyond habitual methods. As an intervision group, we further aspire to contribute ongoing best-practice recommendations that simplify daily challenges in a demanding and often isolated profession.

Key words: Sport Psychology, approaches, injury, international intervision group

articles.title: MEMORY REACTIVATION ALTERS THE FATE OF NEUTRAL EPISODIC MEMORIES FOLLOWING A SUBSEQUENT INDEPENDENT EXPERIENCE
articles.authors: Malen D. Moyano; Jingyi Wang; Luis Brusco; Cecilia Forcato
articles.abstract: Memory reactivation may lead to strengthening, weakening, or updating depending on the experience that follows retrieval. Although post-reactivation modification has been shown for emotional, aversive, and naturalistic episodic memories, it remains unclear whether a consolidated neutral memory for an everyday-like event can be distorted when reactivation is followed by a subsequent independent episodic experience. Yet memories that later become relevant for testimony often initially concern neutral everyday events, such as conversations, routine encounters, or the presence of a person in a given context. Here, we examined whether a consolidated complex neutral episodic memory could be modified when reactivation was followed by a subsequent independent episodic experience. Participants encoded a neutral audiovisual story and returned one week later for an incomplete reminder designed to reactivate the original memory. After reactivation, one group encoded a second neutral audiovisual story, whereas another group received the reminder only. Two control groups either encoded the second story without prior reactivation or received no reminder. One week later, memory was assessed using free recall, cued recall, recognition, and temporal order tasks. Reactivation followed by the second episodic experience reduced accurate recall of the original story and increased false recall and intrusions from the subsequent story. In contrast, reminder-only reactivation was associated with better preservation and fewer distortions. These effects were expressed primarily in free recall. Thus, the fate of a consolidated complex neutral episodic memory depended on post-reactivation experience, with reactivation alone associated with relative preservation and reactivation followed by a new independent episode promoting updating/interference.

articles.title: Principled Default Priors for Bayesian Hypothesis Testing in Binomial GLMs:   A Matched-Prior Framework with Empirical Evaluation
articles.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn; Joscha Dutli; Philipp Musfeld; Klaus Oberauer
articles.abstract: Researchers using Bayesian hypothesis testing in binomial generalized linear models (GLMs; for instance, logistic regression for accuracy data) need priors on regression coefficients, but no widely adopted default framework exists. The nonlinear link function creates a prior-link interaction: priors that appear reasonable on the coefficient scale can imply implausible distributions on the probability scale. We show that this problem has an exact solution for CDF-based link functions: matched priors – prior families whose CDF mirrors the link function – produce uniform distributions on the probability scale for the intercept, a maximally uninformative anchor. We extend this family choice to effect priors for parsimony, with prior scale determined via prior predictive simulation. We embed this matched-prior principle in a three-step workflow and evaluate it via simulation: (1) identify matched priors, (2) evaluate prior predictive distributions, (3) calibrate Bayes factors and compare to the JZS/Cauchy default. For logistic regression, the matched Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept prior and matched Logistic effect priors with scale 0.25 to 0.30 provide well-calibrated Bayes factors. A signal detection analysis shows that prior scale is a criterion parameter: it shifts the operating point on the ROC curve but does not change discriminability. The advantage of the matched-prior workflow is principled scale selection on the probability scale, where effect sizes are directly interpretable. The workflow extends naturally to hierarchical models, where the prior on the random-effects variance has negligible influence on Bayes factors for fixed effects. Ready-to-use brms code and scaling formulas for any contrast coding are provided.

articles.title: Falling on Fertile Ground: National Identity Rhetoric Mobilises Those High in National Narcissism
articles.authors: Chiara Zazzarino; Stefan Leach; Aleksandra Cislak; Magdalena Formanowicz; Jan Nikadon; Aleksandra Cichocka
articles.abstract: Politicians frequently talk about national identity and commitment to national interests. We examined whether such rhetoric mobilises supporters by exploring the role of national narcissism—a belief that one’s nation is exceptional and entitled to special treatment. We tested whether national identity rhetoric boosts the audience’s national narcissism or whether it appeals to those already high in national narcissism. In six experiments, conducted in the US and UK (Ntotal = 3,716), we measured reactions to AI-generated political speeches (Studies 1, 3, 4 and 6) and social media posts (Studies 2 and 5). We found that participants high in national narcissism perceived messages promoting national identity as more persuasive and were more willing to share them on social media, compared to messages rejecting national identity (Studies 1 and 2) or neutral ones (Studies 3 and 4). We also found that national narcissism predicted voting for (Studies 1 and 3), and broadly supporting (Studies 4 and 6), leaders who appealed to national identity in their speeches, compared to those who did not. In Study 5, we corroborated our findings by relying on behavioural indices of engagement with social media posts on a mock platform. Similar effects were observed for messages promoting national identification and national narcissism. Furthermore, in Study 6, national narcissism predicted support for leaders promoting (vs. rejecting) national narcissism regardless of their partisan affiliation (as Republican vs. Democrat). Across the six studies, we found no reliable evidence that national identity messages affected participants’ own national sentiments.

articles.title: Diving into the stigma around consensual non-monogamies: Comparing psychopathology, well-being, attachment, and other psychological characteristics with monogamous counterparts
articles.authors: Oscar Lecuona; Magy García-Senle; Paula Serrano; Rocío Iturri; Irene Martínez-Cuevas; Mireya Brito; Sara de Rivas
articles.abstract:
Objectives
This study aims to empirically challenge pervasive stigma and stereotypes around Consensual Non-Monogamy (CNM) by comprehensively comparing the psychological profiles of CNM practitioners and monogamous individuals, examining both stigma-related factors and psychological resources, while exploring the intersectional role of LGBTQIA+ identity. 
Method
Using a cross-sectional design, 815 Spanish adults (388 CNM, 427 monogamous) completed validated self-report measures for all target constructs, with group comparisons conducted via one-way ANCOVAs controlling for age and LGTBIQA+ status. 
Results
Given the small effect sizes observed, interpretations are made with caution. Analyses revealed no robust overall differences in psychopathology or dark personality traits, directly refuting maladjustment stereotypes. CNM practitioners reported significantly higher scores in sexual sensation seeking, resilience, autonomy, and personal growth, alongside lower personal distress. Importantly, intersectional analyses indicated that LGTBIQA+ monogamous individuals exhibited the highest levels of anxious attachment and psychopathology, suggesting CNM may buffer these negative outcomes within the LGBTQIA+ community. 
Conclusions
These findings challenge deficit-based narratives, indicating that CNM is not associated with elevated psychological risk but is linked to psychological strengths. This underscores the necessity for nuanced, evidence-based, and stigma-free frameworks in both research and clinical practice addressing diverse relational orientations.

Keywords: non-monogamy; LGTBIAQ+, polyamory; psychopathology; adult attachment; well-being

articles.title: A Developmental Map of Pathogen-Avoidance Behaviors
articles.authors: Serkan Ozcakan; Florian van Leeuwen; Joshua M. Tybur
articles.abstract:
Despite the significant costs of early-life infections, young children show little behavioral avoidance of pathogens. This phenomenon raises as-of-yet unanswered questions about when anti-pathogen psychology develops. The present cross-sectional study examined parent-reported observations of 39 behaviors from infancy through middle childhood, based on reports from 3,050 parents from the UK and US. Across fine-grained monthly age intervals (0–120 months), distinct developmental trajectories were identified and then grouped into four clusters based on temporal patterns. Behaviors that increased pathogen exposure—such as mouthing and contact with dirty objects—were most frequent during infancy and toddlerhood. Hygiene routines and disgust responses emerged later and remained stable across the observed age range. Two age-related transitions, around the second and fourth years, marked shifts from early exploratory and risk-prone behaviors toward increasingly organized pathogen-avoidant ones. Together, these findings provide a developmental overview of anti-pathogen psychology and clarify when children begin to act in ways that reduce pathogen exposure.

Keywords: pathogen avoidance; development; disgust; hygiene; behavioral immune system

articles.title: Curriculum learning for complex tasks
articles.authors: Tsvetomira Dumbalska; Kinsey Yuen; Areej Bhatti; Ibi Ali; Mirela Zaneva; Kai Sandbrink; Christopher Summerfield
articles.abstract: Learning to solve a complex task involves discovering new concepts and understanding how to use them. Here, we studied how these two aspects of learning should be sequenced to promote effective task acquisition. We designed video games in which different concepts (tools or ingredients) were used sequentially to complete the task (reach a goal or create a potion). During self-directed learning, participants chose to progress via a curriculum that graduated the complexity of concept discovery (number of concepts involved) rather than of concept implementation (number of steps to goal). However, those who chose to graduate the implementation complexity performed better. Three subsequent experiments that randomised participants into curriculum groups confirmed that adjusting the complexity of concept implementation (not discovery) is the more effective learning strategy. When acquiring complex tasks, learners should not attempt to discover new concepts prematurely, but instead focus on practicing those which they have already mastered.

articles.title: Qualitative Study of Well-being at Work among People with Intellectual Disabilities in Sheltered Employment: Perspectives of Workers and their Supervisors
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Meggy Hayotte; Clément Ginoux; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract: Despite its central role in supporting job retention, the well-being of persons with intellectual disabilities in the workplace remains insufficiently documented in the scientific literature. This qualitative study sought to address this gap by contributing to a better understanding of how the concept of well-being at work is experienced by people with disabilities in sheltered employment, drawing on the Demand-Induced Stain Compensation-Recovery model and theories of recovery at work. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 workers with intellectual disabilities and nine supervisors who support them in their daily work to capture their respective perspectives. A rigorous thematic analysis of the transcribed interviews was conducted by combining deductive and inductive approaches with a double-coding of certain interviews. The results globally highlighted the specific nature of job demands and job resources in sheltered employment settings, the presence of work recovery processes, and relevant indicators for assessing well-being at work in this population. In addition, a number of individual factors—either facilitating or limiting—were identified as influencing the workplace experience of this population. These findings, while demonstrating the relevance of the models considered, also underscore the need for future research to empirically test the theoretical relationships, using designs adapted to this population.

articles.title: Svayoga approach to applying Indian psychology for mental health
articles.authors: Jyotsna Agrawal
articles.abstract: The Svayoga approach is predominantly rooted in core yogic texts; the Bhagavad Gita, Patanjali Yogasutra and Yoga Vasistha, and its thematic analysis, which had resulted in a model with seven interlinked themes (Agrawal, 2022). The theme of ‘Yogic perspective’ emphasizes the role of Consciousness, play of triguna, meaning of suffering and cultivation of inner freedom; theme of ‘Self’ differentiates outer and inner self, and provides reflections and practices to find intimacy with one’s deeper self; theme of ‘Experiences’ explores the dynamics of klesha which colors our daily experiences and keeps us stuck, and need for cultivation of anasakti and samata; themes of ‘Sattvic qualities’ focuses on personal growth and self-perfection through discovering as well as developing various positive qualities; theme of ‘Karmayoga’ examines the path of desireless action and its practice in routine life; theme of ‘Interconnection’ discusses the presence of same Consciousness in everyone and developing ethical and harmonious approach to relationships; finally the theme of ‘Divine’ explores various manifestations of sacred, and deepening our personal spirituality. The model has further been expanded with inclusion of parallel ideas from other Indian texts, traditions, as well as writings of saints and mystics to make it more comprehensive and relatable for application. The approach and empirical findings while applying the model for mental health will be discussed in this chapter.

articles.title: Development of Math Anxiety from Fourth to Fifth Grade as a Function of Control-Value Profiles
articles.authors: Anna Tapola; Riikka Mononen; Hans Lehikoinen; Johan Korhonen
articles.abstract: In this study we investigated the development of cognitive and affective math anxiety from fourth to fifth grade in the light of students’ control and value appraisals. Control-value theory (CVT) postulates students’ anxiety to depend partly on the level of control and value perceptions, and their mutual configuration. Accordingly, students (N = 317) were classified based on their control (i.e., self-concept; C) and value (i.e., interest; V) appraisals in mathematics in grade 4 by using latent profile analysis. The development of math anxiety over one school year in the latent profiles was examined by repeated-measures analysis of covariance, with students’ mathematics performance as a covariate. Four groups of students with different CV profiles were identified: high CV (46 %), high C – low V (26 %), moderate C – high V (18 %), and low CV (10 %). The results showed that students in the different groups displayed different developmental patterns in terms of affective math anxiety; anxiety increased only in the group with moderate control but high value appraisals. In contrast, a similar group x time interaction effect was not observed in terms of cognitive math anxiety. Girls were found to be over-represented in groups displaying low or moderate control, thus predisposing them to higher math anxiety. The results emphasize the importance of acknowledging individual variation in the development of math anxiety, and the role students’ relatively stable motivational beliefs play in it.

articles.title: Diving into the Stigma Around Consensual Non-Monogamies: Comparing Psychopathology, Well-Being, Attachment, and Other Psychological Characteristics with Monogamous Counterparts
articles.authors: Oscar Lecuona; Magaly Luisina García Senlle; Paula Serrano; Rocío Iturri; Irene Martínez-Cuevas; Mireya Brito; Sara de Rivas
articles.abstract:
Objectives: This study aims to empirically challenge pervasive stigma and stereotypes around Consensual Non-Monogamy (CNM) by comprehensively comparing the psychological profiles of CNM practitioners and monogamous individuals, examining both stigmarelated factors and psychological resources, while exploring the interactive role of LGBTQIA+ identity.
Method: Using a cross-sectional design, 815 Spanish adults (388 CNM, 427 monogamous) completed validated self report measures for all target constructs, with group comparisons conducted via one-way ANCOVAs controlling for age and LGBTIQA+ status.
Results: Given the small effect sizes observed, interpretations are made with caution. Analyses revealed no robust overall differences in psychopathology or dark personality traits, directly refuting maladjustment stereotypes. CNM practitioners reported significantly higher scores in sexual sensation seeking, resilience, autonomy, and personal growth, alongside lower personal distress. Importantly, interaction analyses indicated that LGBTIQA+ monogamous individuals exhibited the highest levels of anxious attachment and psychopathology. Relationship style interacted significantly with LGBTQIA+ identity across several outcomes
Conclusions: Overall, the findings do not support deficit-based accounts portraying CNM as inherently associated with greater psychological risk. Instead, the pattern observed in this sample was largely one of psychological similarity, with some small differences favoring CNM participants on selected resource-related variables. These results support the need for nuanced, evidence-based, and stigma-free frameworks in research and clinical practice addressing diverse relational orientations.

articles.title: Evaluating 𝑑′: Global Motion Detection requires Random Scale Representation and Allows for Threshold Representation
articles.authors: Ruby; Henrik Singmann
articles.abstract:
Global motion detection performance is often described via 𝑑′
(i.e., equal-variance Gaussian Signal Detection Theory), despite
evidence that global motion detection requires a threshold
representation which is incompatible with 𝑑′. Both 𝑑′ and
threshold representation share the core assumption of randomscale
representation (RSR), which posits a latent evidence scale
without committing to specific distributional forms. We apply
critical tests to assess whether global motion detection requires
a RSR and whether a threshold representation is admissible.
Participants completed an 𝑚-alternative forced-choice random
dot motion task with 𝑚 = {2 . . . 8}. Accuracy across 𝑚 satisfied
RSR constraints, providing strong evidence that global
motion detection relies on RSR. We derived a hazard function
from the accuracy and tested the monotonicity constraint
implied by threshold representation. The hazard function satisfied
monotonicity, consistent with a threshold account. Reconstructed
ROC curves were piece-wise linear, inconsistent with
equal-variance Gaussian SDT, while generally consistent with
threshold models.

articles.title: Evaluation of the Social Media Minimum Age on Australian Young People: A Study Protocol
articles.authors: Anja Stevic; Y. Anthony Chen; Angela Yuson Lee; Xun Liu; Zacariah Smith-Russack; Kathryn Cairns; Bianca Kahl; Mariesa Nicholas; Isabella Hall; Theebana Tharmakumar
articles.abstract: Australia implemented the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth; SMMA) on December 10, 2025. This policy represents a world-first social media age-restriction, which requires age-restricted social media platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent Australians under the age of 16 from creating or keeping an account. Preliminary estimates suggest that approximately 1,194,000 young people will be affected by the deactivation of accounts. As the SMMA is enacted, we are collecting data to examine the outcomes for young people, parents, and families. This study protocol paper serves as a summary of the methodological design for the evaluation of the implementation and outcomes of the SMMA, including a) young people’s adherence, and the SMMA’s impact on b) their digital practices, c) their physical, psychological, and social wellbeing, d) their families, and e) community attitudes and dynamics. To evaluate the impact of the SMMA implementation, a mixed-methods approach is being undertaken involving 4,121 young people aged 10 to 16 years and their parents or caregivers. Data collection involves longitudinal parent-child surveys, opt-in passive smartphone tracking, administrative data, qualitative interviews, focus groups and diary studies. Findings from this evaluation will inform national policy oversight and implementation in Australia;  contribute empirical evidence to international debates; and inform other countries considering similar age-based regulation of social media. Results will be disseminated through public-facing reports, peer-reviewed publications, and stakeholder engagement activities to support evidence-informed decision-making in digital safety regulation in Australia and internationally.

articles.title: Cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence: a scoping review of performance, perceptions, and intentions
articles.authors: Martina Vacondio; Nicola Vasta; Claudio Mulatti; Francesco Biondi
articles.abstract:
Cognitive offloading, the practice of utilizing external tools to reduce mental demand, is
shifting from traditional memory aids to artificial intelligence (AI). While traditional offloading
is typically associated with lower-order cognitive tasks, AI facilitates the delegation of
complex, higher-order processes. Despite rapid adoption, the downstream consequences of
offloading to AI remain under-explored and evidence is mixed. Following PRISMA-SCR
guidelines, this scoping review synthesizes 20 empirical studies (2023–2025) to provide a
picture of this evolving field. We propose a categorization of the extant research into three
distinct domains: (1) intentions to offload, (2) effects on cognitive performance, and (3)
perceptions and beliefs. This framework serves as a tool for monitoring the rapid development
of cognitive offloading to AI and addressing the current difficulty of interpreting heterogeneous
approaches across the literature. Results reveal generally positive attitudes and high usage
intentions. While performance appears to increase during AI-assisted tasks, participants often
show no performance advantage compared to non-users once tools are removed. All studies
evaluating critical thinking report negative effects, suggesting a cognitive trade-off. To navigate
these complexities, we outline a future research agenda that emphasizes the need for
longitudinal investigations, as well as larger and more diverse participant samples.

articles.title: Behavioral biomarker reliability can mislead mechanistic inference in precision psychiatry
articles.authors: Kenny Yu; Maria Martinovna Robinson; wolf vanpaemel; francis tuerlinckx; Jonas Zaman
articles.abstract: Psychological tasks are increasingly used to develop behavioral biomarkers for precision psychiatry, yet poor test-retest reliability of many task-derived summary measures has raised doubts about their use for stratifying patients, predicting treatment response or indexing clinically relevant mechanisms. In simulations of a fear-conditioning task, we establish two results. First, common summaries can mislead in two ways: they can appear unreliable because they are shaped by experimental context, such as trial order, or reliable because they capture stable but unintended features of responding rather than the target mechanism. Second, computational-model parameters can support stronger reliability claims when they more closely track the intended process, provided the model captures the underlying mechanism and the design makes it recoverable. Together, these findings show that reliability can systematically mislead mechanistic inference unless interpreted with respect to a generative model, the diagnosticity of the task design and assumptions linking the metric to the intended mechanism.

articles.title: Associations between social cognition measures and alcohol use across age and sex: a network approach
articles.authors: Christophe Romein; Emese Kroon; Karis Colyer-Patel; René Freichel; Helle Larsen; Janna Cousijn
articles.abstract: Background: Despite the importance of social factors in the initiation and escalation of alcohol use, social processes related to alcohol use severity are typically studied in isolation. Because real-world social processes occur concurrently and may interact with one another as well as with age and sex, a network approach may provide a more ecologically valid framework. Hence, we used a network approach to examine associations between different social cognition measures and alcohol use severity, while also assessing the roles of age and sex. Methods: Alcohol users (N=936; 16-81yrs) completed the social and conformity subscales of the Drinking Motives Questionnaire Revised, the Social Reward Questionnaire, the Social Attunement Questionnaire, and measures of alcohol use severity. Using network analysis, we examined unique associations between social measures and alcohol use severity, the moderating role of age, and sex differences. Results: Alcohol use severity was linked to social drinking motives and sociability (i.e., the tendency to participate in social gatherings). In the age-moderated network, associations were largely stable across age, except for the association between sociability and alcohol use severity, which was weaker in older participants. We found no sex differences in the pattern of associations. Discussion: Alcohol use severity was primarily associated with general social engagement, while more specific social-cognitive measures were only indirectly related. Social drinking contexts may therefore be a key pathway to greater severity, especially in younger drinkers. Associations did not differ by sex, suggesting previously reported sex differences may reflect differences in prevalence, rather than sex moderating social factors.

articles.title: Exploring diagnosis of Developmental Coordination Disorder and  Specific Developmental Disorder of Motor Function: a secondary data analysis using Connected Bradford
articles.authors: Lucy H Eddy; Matthew Warburton; Cara E Staniforth; Megan L Wood; Liam Hill; Mark Mon-Williams
articles.abstract: Background: Approximately 5% of children are affected by a neurodevelopmental disorder of their sensorimotor skills. DSM-V and ICD-10, the two most widely used classifications systems, define this diagnostically as either ‘Developmental Coordination Disorder’ (DCD) or ‘Specific Developmental Disorder of Motor Function’ (SDDMF, respectively). Being diagnosed with DCD/SDDMF has been found to have a detrimental impact on long-term health and education outcomes. Research repeatedly highlights parental dissatisfaction with the pathways for assessment and support of DCD/SDDMF, however, there has been a lack of research quantitatively exploring the diagnostic landscape. This study therefore aimed to evaluate the incidence of DCD/SDDMF in a diverse District (Bradford, UK) from 1950 -December 2024. Methods: Clinical codes related to sensorimotor skill assessments and diagnoses were searched for within the Connected Bradford dataset, which houses routinely collected primary and secondary healthcare data for over 800,000 residents. Results: There are 182,978 children currently in the Connected Bradford primary care records, suggesting there should be ~9149 children with a diagnosis (given estimated prevalence rates of 5%). But over 74 years of records available, there were only 152 recorded childhood diagnoses of SDDMF (the ICD-10 used in the UK and Europe for diagnosis). When exploring related diagnoses and findings there were 1037 cases (~14 per year), however this amount over 74 years is still nine times lower than would be expected within current childhood populations in Bradford. Moreover, there were low levels of recorded assessments and a lack of clarity regarding how children are being assessed. Conclusion: Diagnosis is the current pathway to accessing support across UK services, yet the current study highlights that children with DCD/SDDMF are not being diagnosed within Bradford. This likely reflects national and international challenges. Further research is needed to investigate the barriers and facilitators to assessing, diagnosing, and supporting children with DCD/SDDMF.

articles.title: What Makes a Habit? Investigating Potential Determinants of Habit Formation
articles.authors: Sebastian Bürgler; Marina Milyavskaya; Gail McMillan; Rachel J Burns; Phillippa Lally; Benjamin Gardner
articles.abstract: Habitual behaviors are automatic responses to specific cues, acquired through repetition in stable contexts. While habits can support long-term behavior change, relatively little is known about which factors influence their development. We conducted a preregistered reanalysis of a six-month longitudinal study on habit formation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants (N = 254) completed monthly surveys assessing behavioral automaticity (i.e., habit) and ten potential determinants. Cluster analyses revealed two trajectories: habit formation and habit degradation, with cluster membership differing by behavioral complexity, frequency, and context stability. Multilevel models showed that six determinants were significantly associated with habit strength: autonomous motivation, behavior frequency, context stability, feeling energized, feeling pleased (positive), and perceived difficulty (negative). A significant interaction between time and behavior frequency emerged after correcting for multiple testing. Findings underscore the dynamic nature of habits and suggest that tailored interventions may be especially important during early formation and to prevent later degradation.

articles.title: The Relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Emotion Regulation: A Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Hester Xiao; Kit S Double; Rebecca Pinkus; Muuskan Kalwani; Riley Leckie; Carolyn MacCann
articles.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) reflects individuals’ capacities, whereas emotion regulation involves the behaviours people use to manage emotions. This meta-analysis (n = 115 studies, k = 923 effects) examined associations between EI and 20 common regulation processes, considering three major EI streams and four ability branches. EI was positively associated with putatively adaptive processes (direct situation modification, positive reappraisal, deep acting, seeking help), negatively associated with putatively maladaptive processes (avoidance, denial, surface acting, catastrophizing, self-blame, expressive suppression, substance use), and positively associated with religious coping and humor. EI stream moderated effects for direct situation modification, acceptance, positive reappraisal, distraction, and seeking help (weaker for ability EI than other streams; weaker for mixed EI than self-rated EI). EI branch moderated associations of ability EI with direct situation modification and seeking help, with stronger effects for emotion management. Overall, findings indicate that emotionally intelligent individuals primarily regulate emotions by addressing problems (direct modification, seeking help) or reframing situations (positive reappraisal), reflecting a tendency to use engagement rather than disengagement regulation processes. Test format (ability vs. rating scale) and theoretical model (ability vs. mixed) significantly influenced effect sizes. This meta-analysis advances understanding of emotion regulation as a key pathway linking EI to positive outcomes.

articles.title: Development, Content Validation, and Preliminary Accessibility Testing of a Workplace Well-Being Assessment Tool for Workers with Intellectual Disabilities
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Pascale Leconte; Marine Peslier; Sophie Posseme; Anne Palanque; Tiphaine Huyghebaert-Zouaghi; Nolwenn Charles; Julio César Alves Da Silva; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract:
Background: Workplace well-being is a critical determinant of job retention for people with intellectual disabilities. Despite its importance, no validated instrument exists to assess this construct among these workers. The objective of the present research was therefore to develop a battery of questionnaire tailored to people with intellectual disabilities in sheltered employment to assess workplace well-being and its associated factors. Furthermore, this study aimed to provide evidence regarding the instrument's content validity and initial evidence of its accessibility for the target population.
Method: In a first study, the content of the developed questionnaire battery was evaluated by an expert committee using the Lynn method. The instrument included four indicators of workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, need for recovery, vigor, job satisfaction), job characteristics (i.e., job demands and job resources), and off-duty recovery (i.e., recovery activities and experiences), variables based on the JD-R model, DISC-R model and recovery theories. In a second study, this validated questionnaire was administered to 29 participants to assess its accessibility.
Results: All 80 items developed received content validation by the expert committee. The pilot study conducted with the target population provided initial evidence of the instrument accessibility.
Conclusion: Further research is needed to test the questionnaire with a larger sample to provide psychometric evidence and additional evidence of its accessibility for workers with intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: From Review to Synthesis: A Step-by-Step Methodological Guide to Systematic Reviews and Multilevel Meta- Analyses
articles.authors: Hu Meilan; Paye Shin Koh; Xun Ci Soh; Andree Hartanto; Nadyanna M. Majeed
articles.abstract: We provide a step-by-step guide on conducting a quantitative systematic review (i.e., meta-analysis) using the open-source programming language R, as well as conducting a multilevel meta-analysis, in contexts where effect sizes are non-independent (e.g., multiple effect studies from the same lab). Quantitative systematic reviews offer researchers a method to synthesise large bodies of literature, helping to clarify inconsistent findings, identify research gaps, and refine theoretical models. However, existing tutorials often assume prior knowledge and/or experience, often overlooking foundational concepts. To address this gap, a comprehensive walkthrough of the systematic review process is presented, covering pre-registration, literature search and retrieval, screening, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction following the PRISMA framework. We then present detailed guidance on how to conduct both traditional and multilevel meta-analyses in R. Specifically, the tutorial explains how to estimate overall meta-analytic effect sizes when effect sizes are independent (traditional meta-analysis) and when effect sizes are nested within labs (multilevel meta-analysis). Procedures for assessing heterogeneity, testing for publication bias, and conducting moderation analyses are also covered. To accompany this tutorial, we supplement annotated R scripts and R notebooks to support transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for researchers of all levels of experience.

articles.title: Natural language correlates of prior suicidal experiences in stream-of-consciousness writing
articles.authors: Soren Wainio-Theberge; Yifan Chen; Caiden Royce; Nina Micanovic; Jeremy Gordon Stewart; Ryan L. Boyd; Vera Vine
articles.abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) can detect suicide risk when trained on explicit discussions of suicide. However, analyzing such texts prevents researchers from understanding the fingerprints of suicide-related cognition in everyday life, before and outside of suicidal crises. We used data-driven analyses to examine links between histories of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) and NLP applied to stream-of-consciousness writing. In a young adult sample enriched in STBs (N=421), we found that negative internally-oriented cognition, references to ambivalent affect in interpersonal relationships, and a disinhibited writing style expressing unmet needs were all associated with participants’ histories of ideation, plans, and attempts. Links between identified linguistic components and STBs were present regardless of whether texts were about suicide. Linguistic components were weakly related to measures of psychopathology and trait affect, suggesting some independence. This is one of the first uses of NLP to understand the implicit mental processes that may contribute to suicide.

articles.title: Open MDMA: An Evidence-Based Synthesis, Theory, and Manual for MDMA Therapy Based on Memory Reconsolidation, Complex Systems, and the Defense Cascade
articles.authors: Mark Groeneveld
articles.abstract:
MDMA therapy is not approved by most medical regulators. But underground use is popular despite a severe lack of adequate practical guidance. Thus, I provide comprehensive practical guidance for solo and guided MDMA therapy based on critical literature synthesis, personal experience, community reports, and a mechanistic framework. I primarily address the individual doing or seeking MDMA therapy while also discussing certain aspects mostly of interest to practitioners and researchers. With this manual I aim to improve the appeal, safety, and efficacy of MDMA therapy through scientific rigor, comprehensiveness, transparency, and respect for autonomy.

These ideas are grounded in a theoretical model based on frameworks of memory reconsolidation, predictive processing, complex system dynamics, and the defense cascade model of autonomic nervous system threat responses. I use this to explain how many mental illnesses work, how MDMA therapy works, why destabilization exists, and how to navigate the long-term healing process. I argue that MDMA therapy durably improves many mental illnesses and stuck emotional reactions and beliefs through the unlearning, or reconsolidation, of inaccurate mental models. It reconsolidates most or all stuck mental models that are activated---and which you stay present with---during the session.

Practical guidance contains evidence-based discussion of safety, session preparation, the session itself, troubleshooting, between-session healing, and how that all fits into the longer-term healing journey. I also extend MDMA therapy beyond clinical mental illness to mental models that inhibit healthy community relationships, cognitive flexibility, and ethical reasoning. The tradeoffs between practitioner- versus self-guidance and instructions on how to find skilled, ethical, and well-matched practitioners are included.

This is the only MDMA/psychedelic therapy manual to explain and justify its recommendations based on a mechanistic theory of mental illness and healing while providing reasons for both confidence and skepticism of its claims.

articles.title: Virtual Reality Gaming as a Non-Pharmacological Intervention for Pain Management During Medical Procedures: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Marie SZABELSKI; Matthieu BURTIN; Matthieu CASTERAN
articles.abstract:
Background
The virtual reality is an increasingly used technology for pain and anxiety management in patients. This study focuses on the effectiveness and safety of virtual reality games for these purposes.

Methods
The literature search was conducted until November 1, 2025. Four databases were used to identify relevant randomized controlled trial published between 2000 and 2025 concerning the use of virtual reality video games to reduce pain and anxiety or to improve stakeholder satisfaction (patients, caregivers and/or parents). The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the PEDro scales.

Results
A total of 963 articles was identified, of which 54 full-text meet the inclusion criteria. These studies addressed both intra-operative and post-operative pain. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across studies regarding patient populations (children or adults), game content (active, passive, or mixed; specific or non-specific), and types of medical procedures.

Conclusion
The reviewed studies indicate that virtual reality can be safely used during a wide range of medical procedures, more or less painful. Although data collected do not provide consistent and robust evidence for a significant reduction in drug consumption or anxiety level, the majority of studies reported positive results in terms of pain reduction through the use of virtual reality games, demonstrating the potential effectiveness of this technology as a therapeutic support during medical procedure. Moreover, the analysis of the heterogeneity of the results shows that studies reporting a significant reduction in pain are more common when the content is specifically designed for pain management and adapted for the target population. This observation points to the relevance of content specificity and user-centered design in maximizing therapeutic outcomes. Future research could further explore the differences between traditional games and games specifically designed for pain management, with the aim of optimizing their analgesic effect.

articles.title: What is Evaluative Conditioning Anyway? A Response to De Houwer (2026)
articles.authors: Olivier Corneille; Jérémy Béna
articles.abstract: We respond to De Houwer's (2026) commentary on our preprint (Corneille et al., 2026). In that preprint, we proposed a new definition of the Evaluative Conditioning effect (ECe) to address what we see as limitations in how ECe is currently conceptualized and studied. In the present response, we discuss substantive agreements and disagreements with De Houwer's commentary and clarify apparent misunderstandings on both sides. In doing so, we argue that our proposed definition withstands De Houwer's counter-arguments and offers a sensible alternative to existing definitions. More broadly, we believe that this exchange highlights important conceptual, methodological, and measurement-related questions whose resolution may have far-reaching implications for EC research. We hope that the discussion of these issues lives on beyond this exchange and helps move the field forward.

articles.title: Representational Inconsistency: Understanding When to Re-evaluate Decisions
articles.authors: Eeshan Hasan; Jennifer S Trueblood
articles.abstract: Decision errors are often classified as noise or bias, yet little guidance exists for identifying the source of a specific decision error. We propose that this distinction can be inferred from the local structure of an observer’s decision space. Responses to similar stimuli reveal a latent decision space—a probabilistic mapping from representational structure to categorical decisions—against which individual decisions can be evaluated. An error is representationally inconsistent when the observed response is unlikely given the observer’s previous decisions on similar stimuli, reflecting a noise-like departure from the observer’s own decision space. In contrast, representationally consistent errors reflect stable, bias-like regularities within that structure. We formalize this framework using similarity-based models of categorization. Representational structure is operationalized using deep neural network embeddings, and an individual’s decision space is estimated by weighting prior decisions according to representational similarity. The framework predicts that representationally inconsistent errors should be more likely to be corrected through re-evaluation, whereas representationally consistent errors should tend to persist. We demonstrate these predictions in medical image classification tasks involving novice and expert decision makers. Building on this principle, we derive aggregation and selective re-sampling algorithms that reduce error by targeting locally inconsistent judgments and show how the framework can guide whether repeated evaluation or second opinions are more likely to improve decisions. These findings establish representational inconsistency as a computational marker of correctable error, integrating similarity-based theories of categorization with a broader account of judgment revision, decision aggregation, and the sources of human error.

articles.title: Causal Effects of Beliefs About Errors on Primary School Students’ Reactions to Errors and Knowledge Acquisition: Evidence from Three Experimental Field Studies
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Andrew Martin; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: Errors occur frequently during educational practice and hold substantial potential for personal improvement. However, learning from errors does not happen automatically; rather, students must react adaptively to their errors and modify the learning process accordingly. Such adaptive reactions to errors involve maintaining learning motivation and functional emotions as well as engaging in cognitive and behavioral adjustment. Although previous research has identified positive beliefs about errors as a potential determinant of adaptive reactions to errors, most evidence is correlational, and experimental investigations—particularly among primary school students—remain limited. Therefore, we conducted three experimental field studies in which we positively manipulated the beliefs about errors in an experimental group which was compared to an active control group. In an authentic learning situation, the utilization of a digital learning environment enabled the observation of both learning behavior and immediate learning progress. In samples of third- and fourth-grade students, Study 1 (N = 282) and Study 2 (N = 238) were conducted in math, while Study 3 (N = 230) focused on German as a first language. The experimental manipulation successfully affected the beliefs about errors in a sustainable manner in all three studies. In turn, positive beliefs about errors improved self-reported adaptive reactions to errors, which was mostly maintained until a follow-up assessment. Additionally, positive beliefs about errors led to a more adaptive learning behavior and greater knowledge acquisition in Study 3. These findings provide novel insights into how positive beliefs about errors influence effective learning from errors.

articles.title: Routine safety narratives reveal dynamic traces of organisational climate
articles.authors: Michael Alan Rosen; Molly Kilcullen; Yuxin Zhu
articles.abstract: ‘Safety climate’ refers to the shared attitudes about safety within an organisation. While traditionally measured via self-report surveys, it can now be measured by analysing the language in written incident reports. Using large-language model-based machine text analysis, we examined whether text-derived measures predict future safety outcomes in four high-risk industries (i.e., rail, nuclear, mining and aviation) and found that safety climate operates through two distinct pathways. First, stronger safety climate predicts less harm and operational failures, suggesting a preventative effect. Second, a stronger safety climate predicts more formal reporting and documentation, reflecting a culture in which workers feel comfortable raising concerns. To ensure these findings were not analytical artefacts, we tested 810 reasonable variations of each analysis using held-out data for validation. Some findings proved robust across all approaches; others depended on specific methodological decisions. This framework demonstrates how organisations can use large-language model-based text analysis to track safety culture dynamically, while validating these measures against real-world outcomes.

articles.title: Multi-System Brain-Body Mechanisms of Mental Health in Long-Term Meditation: Toward a Science of Advanced Meditation
articles.authors: Idil Sezer; Terje Sparby; Kamlesh Chalise; Vanessa Naughton; Matthew Sacchet
articles.abstract:
Most research on meditation and mental health has focused on short-term interventions in
novice populations, leaving the cumulative effects of long-term and advanced practice
underexplored. Advanced meditation is defined as states, stages, and endpoints that arise with the
maturation and mastery of mental-activity skills. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from
52 studies across four databases, examining mental health outcomes through an integrative brain–
body lens.
Six interrelated domains emerged: (1) well-being, (2) interpersonal functioning, (3) emotion
regulation, (4) sensory–affective uncoupling of pain, (5) stress resilience, and (6) psychiatric
symptom prevention. Rather than operating independently, these domains reflect a coordinated,
multi-system adaptive response. Long-term meditation is consistently linked to enhanced
attentional control, reduced emotional reactivity, and increased compassion, changes supported by
functional and structural neuroplasticity in default-mode, salience, and frontoparietal networks.
Emerging evidence further suggests that advanced practitioners may exhibit qualitatively distinct
neural patterns, including reduced self-referential processing and concentration-related states.
Evidence points to benefits beyond the brain. These neural changes are paralleled by
systemic adaptations: modulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenocortical axis,
downregulation of inflammatory gene expression, and upregulation of neuroplasticity-related
molecular markers.
Together, these findings support a holistic framework in which sustained meditation
strengthens interconnected neural, endocrine, immune, and cellular systems that collectively
support mental health and resilience. Meditation is therefore best understood not as a purely
cognitive technique but as a systemic brain–body intervention. Future research should prioritize
longitudinal, mechanistic designs and move beyond duration-based definitions toward skill-based
characterizations of advanced meditation.

articles.title: What is critical metascience and why is it important?
articles.authors: Mark Rubin
articles.abstract: Metascience uses a scientific approach to understand and improve science. Critical metascience takes a step back to question metascience’s commonly-accepted assumptions, methods, problems, and solutions. In this article, I define critical metascience and explain how it can help to identify and address collective biases within metascience. I also highlight some emerging themes in the field. Finally, I consider some potential relationships between metascience and critical metascience and argue that the most functional model is one in which two fields are partially overlapping. I conclude that there needs to be greater recognition and dialogue between metascience and critical metascience in order to improve metascience’s objectivity and approach.

articles.title: Operationalization of Child Abuse and Neglect in ABCD Following WHO guidelines
articles.authors: Suzanne C. Perkins
articles.abstract: A recent paper published in BMC Medical Research Methodology proposed specific variables for the operationalization of early life adversity (ELA) using the adverse childhood experiences (ACE) framework. Although laudable, the operationalization was incorrect regarding child abuse and neglect. Poor operationalization of abuse and neglect will lead to the over-identification of poor youth and youth of color. Following national and international standards for the identification of child abuse and neglect, critiques of the approach are detailed, and readers are referred to the Perkins Framework.

articles.title: Working with Circular Data: A Tutorial for Cognitive and Behavioral Research
articles.authors: Stella Wernicke; Julie de Falco; Zahara Gironés; Chris Jungerius; Ivan Tomic; Adam Triabhall; Xiaolu Wang; Paul Bays
articles.abstract: Introductory statistics courses and conventional methods in behavioral and cognitive science are typically restricted to Euclidean space without explicitly stating this, leaving many researchers unaware of how to handle data with circular or periodic properties (e.g., time of day or orientation on a screen). This tutorial provides an accessible yet rigorous introduction, designed to bridge the gap between statistical theory and practical application. After discussing different ways of representing circular data mathematically and fundamental principles for working with them, we explain angular and vector representations and operations, including key considerations for implementing them in computer code. We then survey methods for visualizing circular data, including linear and polar plots and presentation of summary statistics. Next, we introduce circular measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape: how they relate to their Euclidean counterparts, and why they differ. Finally, we turn to more advanced topics of the kind needed to construct models of circular data. We introduce the most common circular distribution families, including circular analogs of the Gaussian distribution and their properties, as well as flexible distribution families that can describe skewed and heavy-tailed data. We survey common applications in the supplementary materials. The tutorial takes a method-oriented approach, not tied to specific software, but highlighting factors relevant to experimental design, data analysis, and statistical modeling. A consistent theme is the need to rigorously account for the inherent periodicity of circular data. We also provide a consistent notation for circular statistics and parameters, addressing the lack of established conventions in the field.

articles.title: Effects of Cognitive Warmup on Cognitive Performance
articles.authors: Silvia Gobbo; Giorgia Calvetti; Giorgia Tosi; Daniele Romano
articles.abstract: Cognitive performance is composed of a relatively stable cognitive ability (trait) and transient factors (state). While the trait can be influenced by long-term training, transient factors can be manipulated to achieve short-term improvements. Acute physical exercise has shown to improve subsequent cognitive performance through a warm-up effect; however, it remains unclear whether a similar enhancement can be achieved through cognitive activity itself. The present study investigated whether a brief cognitive warm-up could influence subsequent performance on a neuropsychological measure of processing speed. Forty healthy young adults participated in two experimental sessions and were assigned either to a cognitive warm-up group or a no-warm-up control group. The warm-up consisted of a brief series of serious games targeting executive functions and attention. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT). Bayesian analyses indicated an interaction between session and group, with better results for the warm-up group in the active session with respect to the control group, net of scores in Raven’s Matrices. These findings provide preliminary evidence that a brief cognitive warm-up may enhance subsequent performance on a speeded cognitive task. Importantly, the effect emerged in the absence of task-specific priming and did not rely on physical exercise, suggesting that cognitive performance may be influenced through transient modulation of cognitive state. Further research employing active control conditions, larger samples, and direct measures of underlying mechanisms is needed to establish the robustness and specificity of this effect.

articles.title: Multilevel Models: A Tutorial on Applications and Uses in Human Factors Research
articles.authors: Courtney Michael Goodridge; Jac Billington; Gustav Markkula; Richard Wilkie
articles.abstract: Human behaviour is heterogeneous, a feature that is particularly important in Human Factors (HF) research where performance variability can have safety-critical implications. However, HF studies often focus on average effects between experimental conditions, treating individual differences as statistical noise rather than as meaningful information. Modelling behavioural heterogeneity can improve understanding of how systems affect users and support stronger theoretical development. Multilevel Models (MLMs) provide a flexible statistical framework for analysing hierarchical data structures, such as repeated measurements nested within individuals. Advances in statistical software have increased the accessibility of MLMs, yet many HF studies do not fully exploit their ability to model individual differences in experimental effects. One barrier is limited availability of practical tutorials demonstrating how MLMs can be applied to typical HF datasets. This manuscript addresses this gap by providing a practical introduction to MLMs for HF researchers. First, we review MLM principles and their relevance to HF research. We then present two worked examples. Study 1 demonstrates MLMs as an extension of linear regression for continuous predictors; Study 2 applies MLMs to factorial designs and discusses strategies for managing convergence in complex random-effects structures. Analyses are supported by example datasets and code in R, Python, and MATLAB.

articles.title: Using neural signatures to predict health behavior change: A mindful distancing intervention to reduce alcohol consumption as a proof of concept
articles.authors: Danielle Cosme; Chelsea Helion; Yoona Kang; David M. Lydon-Staley; Bruce P Dore; Ovidia Stanoi; Jeesung Ahn; Mia Jovanova; Amanda L. McGowan; Zachary M. Boyd
articles.abstract: Developing interventions to change health behaviors—especially those targeting cross-cutting health risk factors like alcohol use—is a public health priority. In this study, we used a translational neuroscience approach to evaluate the underlying mechanisms and individual differences in a mindful distancing intervention designed to reduce alcohol consumption among college students. We combined functional neuroimaging and machine learning to develop a brain-based predictive model (a “neural signature”) of mindful distancing. This model allowed us to track moment-to-moment variation in how participants implemented the strategy, as well as differences between individuals. Students completed a mindful distancing task involving alcohol cues during fMRI scanning. They then completed a 28-day, smartphone-based, experience sampling intervention. In the laboratory, mindfully attending to alcohol decreased craving, particularly among people who more strongly expressed the mindful distancing signature. In daily life, the mindful distancing intervention increased mindful responses to alcohol and decreased subsequent alcohol consumption through two distinct pathways: mindful responses directly influenced alcohol consumption and indirectly influenced it by reducing cravings for alcohol. Individuals with stronger expression of the neural signature experienced the greatest benefits from the intervention. These findings extend theoretical models of how mindfulness-based emotion regulation strategies impact alcohol use in emerging adults without alcohol use disorders. They also demonstrate the potential of using neural signatures to evaluate health behavior change interventions within a translational neuroscience framework.

articles.title: Ancillary cognitive demands impact children's behavior in common possibility reasoning tasks
articles.authors: Esra Nur Küçük; Stephanie Alderete; Fei Xu; Melissa M. Kibbe
articles.abstract:
The ability to consider multiple, incompatible possibilities supports human decision-making, but there is considerable variability in estimates of the age of emergence and development of this ability in young children. What accounts for this variability? We suggest that one major source is task-specific demands on developing cognitive processes that are not solely dedicated to possibility reasoning. In this paper, we outline a set of ancillary cognitive demands in a variety of common tasks that are currently used to study young children’s possibility reasoning (cups, gumball, slides, branching tube, and playground tasks). We identify five key cognitive demand dimensions – physical reasoning, action planning, working memory, language, and temporal context – and show that these demands can and do impact children’s behaviors in tasks designed to examine possibility reasoning. We discuss implications for understanding the cognitive mechanisms driving possibility reasoning and challenges for identifying developmental trajectories.


Keywords: possibility, uncertainty, reasoning, cognitive demands, cognitive development 

Public Significance Statement: The ability to consider alternative possibilities is essential to human reasoning and decision making. It is therefore important that we understand when and how these abilities develop in early childhood. This paper argues that one major source of developmental variability in possibility reasoning tasks is that different tasks place additional cognitive demands on children, such as action planning and working memory. We provide a framework for identifying and evaluating these ancillary cognitive demands across five commonly used tasks, and show that carefully accounting for them can help researchers interpret children’s behavior more accurately and to design more informative and interpretable studies.

articles.title: Calibrating appropriate trust in human–AI decision-making: The role of system explanations and domain expertise
articles.authors: Katharina Buschmeyer; Sophie Berretta; Sarah Hatfield
articles.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in decision-making raises important questions regarding the factors influencing the trust calibration of users in AI, particularly in situations where errors can have serious consequences. This study examined the effects of global AI system explanations—providing information about cases in which AI is particularly prone to errors—on user experiences and trust behaviour in an art-historical classification task. A total of N = 205 participants with varying domain-specific expertise participated in a randomised Wizard-of-Oz online experiment with a between-subjects design. The results showed that global explanations did not significantly influence decision confidence, perceived psychological load, or appropriate trust calibration and, in some cases, even fostered undertrust among less experienced participants. Domain knowledge emerged as protective factors against inappropriate trust calibrations. This study further emphasises the importance of a nuanced perspective on trust, highlighting the need to distinguish between overtrust, undertrust, and joint misjudgment.

articles.title: Stereotypes of Social Class and Race in the United States: A Social Sampling Account
articles.authors: Salvador Vargas Salfate; Chadly Stern; Benedek Kurdi
articles.abstract: Across five studies (N = 7,075) we use the Implicit Association Test (IAT) to document a stereotype linking White Americans to the trait “rich” and Black Americans to the trait “poor” among Americans of various racial groups. Building on an unexpected finding of stronger White–rich/Black–poor stereotyping among third-group individuals (e.g., Latine and Asian Americans) relative to Black and White Americans, we hypothesized that biased social sampling from network homophily might produce this stereotype. Supporting this possibility, we observed that (a) contact with Black people explained racial group differences in stereotyping and, crucially, (b) exposing participants to counterstereotypic (Black–rich and White–poor) exemplars decreased the degree of stereotyping across a number of procedural variations and to similar degrees across racial groups. Overall, these findings suggest that social relationships are critical to understanding how individuals form and maintain stereotypes about groups that are unequal in wealth and status.

articles.title: Understanding the Hidden Diversity of Socioeconomically Disadvantaged Adolescents: Developmental Pathways of Flourishing and Vulnerability
articles.authors: Azilawati Jamaludin; Aik Lim Tan; Sandeep Singh; Kenneth Poon Kin Loong
articles.abstract: Socioeconomic disadvantage is often associated with poorer developmental outcomes, yet relatively little is known about why adolescents exposed to similar adversity follow markedly different developmental pathways. Drawing on data from the Singapore DREAMS longitudinal cohort (N =7,156), including 1,634 adolescents from the bottom 20% of the socioeconomic strata (B20), this study investigated developmental heterogeneity among socioeconomically disadvantaged students. Latent profile analysis conducted on adolescents with complete psychosocial indicators (n=611) identified five distinct developmental pathways ranging from Broad Psychosocial Vulnerability to Flourishing Despite Disadvantage. Differences in academic attainment and school performance across pathways were statistically significant but modest, whereas psychosocial differences were substantial, often exceeding one standard deviation. Profile membership predicted a wide range of subsequent flourishing outcomes, including academic engagement, academic self-concept, academic buoyancy, identity commitment, connectedness, optimism, and perseverance. Furthermore, flourishing adolescents from disadvantaged backgrounds demonstrated psychosocial functioning largely comparable to flourishing adolescents from more advantaged backgrounds despite occupying dramatically different socioeconomic positions. The findings challenge deficit-oriented accounts of disadvantage and suggest that human flourishing under adversity represents a distinct and measurable developmental phenomenon. Understanding the psychosocial conditions associated with flourishing may be as important as understanding the factors that place adolescents at risk.

articles.title: Building a Beta-Binomial Regression from Summary Data to Identify Reliable Change: Utility for Discrete, Bounded Scores from Neuropsychological Tests
articles.authors: Rafael de Andrade Moral; Javier Oltra-Cucarella; Unai Diaz-Orueta; Rubén Pérez-Elvira; Beatriz Bonete-López; Miriam Sánchez-Sansegundo; Esther Sitges-Maciá
articles.abstract: Standard multiple linear regression is often used to calculate the regression-based Reliable Change Index (RCI) to track longitudinal neuropsychological change. However, the linear model assumes that the response is a continuous, unbounded variable, failing to accommodate the discrete, bounded nature of cognitive test scores that often display overdispersion. Conversely, the beta-binomial (BB) model treats test scores as the number of k successes among m trials and accommodates overdispersion, showing higher positive predictive value to identify dementia compared to the linear model. This study presents a novel approximation method to build beta-binomial (BB) regression models using only summary statistics, which provides researcher and clinicians with a powerful tool to diagnose longitudinal decline. Using longitudinal data from 6,271 cognitively healthy participants from the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center who completed the Craft Story delayed verbatim recall within the Uniform Data Set version 3 or version 4, the BB approximation was evaluated against a full raw-data maximum likelihood framework through 3,000 simulations across different dementia progression prevalences. The BB approximation yielded parameter estimates, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy values nearly identical to the full model, with an 800-fold reduction in computation time. The proposed approximation provides a robust, highly efficient alternative for researchers and clinicians to compute accurate RCIs when raw data are inaccessible. A free website calculator, along with runnable code and a tutorial for the BB approximation with summary data, are provided.

articles.title: Exploring the Impact of Non-Linearity on Effect Heterogeneity in Experimental Data.
articles.authors: Jens Fuenderich; Lukas Joscha Beinhauer; Frank Renkewitz
articles.abstract: Heterogeneity has been proposed as a framework to improve psychological and behavioral science by identifying mechanisms that explain the differences between replications of an effect. The modal response to such differences is to search for relevant moderators—typically with limited success. We argue that monotonic non-linear relationships can generate heterogeneous effects across replications when baseline levels differ, even in the absence of moderators. To evaluate this possibility, we introduce four descriptors of heterogeneity: effect heterogeneity, control group heterogeneity, the intercept–slope correlation, and the rank correlation between control and treatment means. These characterize patterns consistent with linear, concave, or convex functional relationships. We apply this analytical framework to an initial pool of 55 meta-analytic multi-lab data sets. All data sets with heterogeneous effects also demonstrated control group heterogeneity, and several patterns were in line with a concave functional relationship. In some cases, the association between baselines and effects accounted for a substantial proportion of effect heterogeneity. Additionally, only a small number of data sets were directly at odds with a monotonic non-linear functional form. Moreover, our results suggest that effect heterogeneity in multi-lab research reflects diverse data patterns rather than providing support for treating moderators as the modal explanation for effect heterogeneity. We discuss implications for multi-lab and meta-analytic practice, study design, and interpretations of effect heterogeneity. We advocate for a shift from treating only the effect size distribution as the explanandum of the heterogeneity framework to more elaborate descriptions of heterogeneity.

articles.title: Principled Default Priors for Bayesian Hypothesis Testing in Binomial GLMs:   A Matched-Prior Framework with Empirical Evaluation
articles.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn; Joscha Dutli; Philipp Musfeld; Klaus Oberauer
articles.abstract: Researchers using Bayesian hypothesis testing in binomial generalized linear models (GLMs; for instance, logistic regression for accuracy data) need priors on regression coefficients, but no widely adopted default framework exists. The nonlinear link function creates a prior-link interaction: priors that appear reasonable on the coefficient scale can imply implausible distributions on the probability scale. We show that this problem has an exact solution for CDF-based link functions: matched priors – prior families whose CDF mirrors the link function – produce uniform distributions on the probability scale for the intercept, a maximally uninformative anchor. We extend this family choice to effect priors for parsimony, with prior scale determined via prior predictive simulation. We embed this matched-prior principle in a three-step workflow and evaluate it via simulation: (1) identify matched priors, (2) evaluate prior predictive distributions, (3) calibrate Bayes factors and compare to the JZS/Cauchy default. For logistic regression, the matched Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept prior and matched Logistic effect priors with scale 0.25 to 0.30 provide well-calibrated Bayes factors. A signal detection analysis shows that prior scale is a criterion parameter: it shifts the operating point on the ROC curve but does not change discriminability. The advantage of the matched-prior workflow is principled scale selection on the probability scale, where effect sizes are directly interpretable. The workflow extends naturally to hierarchical models, where the prior on the random-effects variance has negligible influence on Bayes factors for fixed effects. Ready-to-use brms code and scaling formulas for any contrast coding are provided.

articles.title: Different post-pandemic patterns in youth mental health and wellbeing after a global stressor: variation across domains and informants
articles.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Hedy van Oers; Cyrina Brouwer; Michiel A.J. Luijten; Jana Runze; Lorynn Teela; Marlene Werner; Josjan Zijlmans; Maaike Oosterling; Hilgo Bruining
articles.abstract:
Objective. The COVID-19 pandemic was a major global stressor for children and adolescents, raising concerns about longer-term consequences for mental health and wellbeing. Many studies reported increased mental health problems during and shortly after the pandemic, but less is known about longer-term post-pandemic patterns across domains and informants.
Method. We used repeated cross-sectional data from Dutch children and adolescents aged 8-18 years in the Netherlands Twin Register (NTR, N = 39,178, 50% girls) and a representative general-population sample (N = 2,782, 48% girls). Parent- and child-reported mental health problems and wellbeing were assessed using pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic data through 2025.
