A key finding is that the residual contributions from measurement error and interaction omission can partially cancel each other out, so that prediction error reduces marginally while leaving coefficient bias large. As a consequence, qualitatively different models can become difficult to distinguish by standard fit metrics, even in large samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate via Monte Carlo simulation that models with more biased estimates can exhibit lower estimator variance, meaning misspecified models may dominate in both inferential and model selection procedures. These results have direct implications for the replicability and interpretability of linear regression models in psychological research.

articles.title: Interictal Epileptiform Discharges and Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Children with Early-Onset Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis
articles.authors: Uffaq Mastoor; Iva Peh; Jemima Alston; Emily Lamcastle; Javier Escudero; Catherine J Crompton; Jayakara Shetty
articles.abstract:
Background: Children with early-onset epilepsy (seizure onset ≤ 5 years) are at elevated risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, including cognitive impairment, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum features. Seizure burden alone provides limited prognostic information. Interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), spike or sharp-wave complexes occurring between clinical seizures on electroencephalography (EEG), are common in paediatric epilepsy and may reflect brain network instability relevant to neurodevelopment. Whether interictal EEG features recorded in early childhood are associated with long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes remains unclear.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with a prospectively registered protocol (PROSPERO: CRD420251162420) and reported per PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, PsycINFO, and Scopus were searched from 1966 to October 2025. Longitudinal studies examining interictal EEG features in children with epilepsy onset ≤ 5 years, with neurodevelopmental outcomes assessed ≥12 months after baseline EEG, were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS; certainty of evidence using GRADE.
Results: Of 1,613 records identified, four longitudinal studies met inclusion criteria (epilepsy contexts: infant-onset focal epilepsy, Sturge–Weber syndrome, epileptic encephalopathies, cryptogenic generalised epilepsies). Across all four studies, greater severity or disruption of interictal EEG activity showed a directional association with poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes. All four studies were rated at moderate to high risk of bias. Certainty of evidence was low to very low across all outcome domains.
Conclusions: Directional evidence links interictal EEG severity to neurodevelopmental outcomes in early-onset epilepsy. However, the evidence base is too sparse, insufficiently standardised, and of too low methodological quality to support definitive prognostic inference. Standardised, state-resolved IED metrics and harmonised outcome batteries are needed to clarify the prognostic role of interictal activity in early-onset epilepsy.
Keywords: epilepsy; interictal epileptiform discharges; electroencephalography; prognosis; neurodevelopment; cognition; paediatric

articles.title: Sensory Processing Sensitivity is associated with Heightened Emotional Response, not Rumination when viewing Climate‑Change Media Content
articles.authors: Annalisa Setti; Catherine Trearty; Anna Oberhaeusser; Anna O'Brien
articles.abstract: Climate change is becoming increasingly recognised as a serious determinant of mental health, with indirect exposure via climate related media eliciting emotional distress and rumination. The present study sought to explore whether sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) moderates responses to climate-related videos, due to higher empathy and depth of processing characterising highly sensitive individuals. In a pre-post experimental design, 119 participants were randomly assigned to view either a climate disaster video or a control weather forecast. Positive affect, negative affect, and rumination were assessed before and after exposure. Results indicated that exposure to climate-related content significantly increased negative affect. SPS moderated this effect, such that individuals higher in sensitivity showed greater increases in negative affect in the climate condition. Nature connectedness also emerged as a significant positive predictor of negative affect, whereas climate change anxiety did not significantly predict outcomes in the final models. Positive affect and rumination were primarily explained by baseline levels and were not significantly influenced by condition or SPS. These findings suggest that negatively valenced climate-related media may elicit distress-related emotional responses, particularly among individuals high in sensory sensitivity, indicating that this dimension is of relevance when studying distressing nature-related situations.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic life, raising important questions about which individuals may be more likely to rely on them when facing challenges. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model linking executive functioning (EF) difficulties to reliance on GenAI, defined as a tendency to depend on GenAI rather than one’s own effort or teacher support when encountering academic challenges, through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage = 17.4 years, 55.2% girls). Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.32, ps < .001). Supporting the hypothesized model, the sequential indirect pathway through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Perceived usefulness emerged as the most consistent mediator, whereas habitual use showed a more limited mediating role despite being strongly associated with reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be a key mechanism linking EF difficulties to reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the role of self-regulatory capacities in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: Handing over control: A longitudinal study of delegation and disclosure in human-AI interaction
articles.authors: Teresa Luther; Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle; Angelica Lermann Henestrosa
articles.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into everyday tasks raises important questions about how individuals rely on these systems in the long run. While prior research has primarily examined cross-sectional predictors of AI use, little is known about how willingness to delegate tasks and disclose information to AI develops over time. The present study addresses this gap examining a six-wave longitudinal survey (N = 1,008 at baseline) conducted over ten months with a U.S. sample. We investigated changes in willingness to delegate professional and personal writing tasks to AI, as well as willingness to disclose information to AI, and tested the influence of user-related (experience, frequency of use, attitudes, and knowledge) and AI-related evaluative factors (trust, anthropomorphism, social actor perception). Contrary to expectations, willingness to delegate and disclose decreased over time, with the decline attenuating across waves. Willingness to delegate remained consistently higher for professional than for personal tasks. Use frequency, positive attitudes, trust, and anthropomorphism were associated with greater willingness to delegate, whereas experience and social actor perception showed no consistent effects. Willingness to disclose was similarly shaped by use and attitudinal factors. These findings suggest that human-AI interaction reflects a process of calibration rather than increasing reliance, highlighting the importance of temporal dynamics in understanding AI adoption and use.

articles.title: No Escape from Behavior in Evaluating Compositionality
articles.authors: Najoung Kim
articles.abstract: Evaluating whether a natural or artificial system exhibits compositionality is an empirical problem of active interest in both Cognitive Science and Artificial Intelligence. Because any function admits some compositional analysis, we need theoretical commitments that clearly define the target function for the question to be well-formed. Which function is appropriate depends on one's domain and scope of inquiry, and no single function is inherently privileged without further independent commitments; the only plausibly universal constraint is that the domain must admit at least one primitive-reuse analysis. Given a properly operationalized notion of compositionality, I argue that there is no escape from behavior in asking whether a system exhibits compositionality. From a constitutive perspective, the complete functional profile is sufficient for the verdict. From an empirical perspective, targeted generalization behavior over withheld recombinations is the critical evidence supporting inductive hypotheses about the function. Contra recent literature arguing that the compositionality verdict should be grounded in mechanistic evidence, mechanism is neither a necessary nor a sufficient adjudicator because it is constitutively subordinate to or evidentially dependent on behavior. Instead, the role of mechanistic evidence is best understood as a bootstrap to the inductive process and an aid to the characterization of the target function. Furthermore, settling the _is-compositional_ question rigorously opens up ways for genuine questions _about_ the mechanism and the behavior-mechanism interface to proceed productively. Finally, this discussion highlights that the critical bottleneck for the _is-compositional_ verdict on contemporary systems is data transparency rather than interpretability.

articles.title: Smoking Exposure Application (SEA): Development and Validation of An Augmented Reality Smoking Cessation App
articles.authors: Reza Barzegar; Javad hatami; Peyman Ghobadi-Azbari; Hamed Ekhtiari; Tara Rezapour
articles.abstract:
Background: Cue-reactivity is a cornerstone of addiction research; however, laboratory-based investigations often lack ecological validity, failing to generalize to real-world experiences. Augmented reality (AR) technology offers a promising solution by bridging the gap between laboratory settings and real-life environments for cue-exposure interventions. 
Objectives: The present study aimed to: (1) develop and validate a set of three-dimensional (3D) smoking-related objects through user evaluation among smokers; and (2) to incorporate these validated images into a smoking cessation application, the Smoking Exposure Application (SEA), designed to elicit cravings within familiar contexts without physical cigarette exposure.
Method: We developed 21 3D objects, including 10 smoking-related cues (e.g., cigarette, ashtray) and 11 control objects (e.g., pencil, gum pack). Forty-five participants (21 smokers and 24 non-smokers) evaluated the objects using the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) to rate valence, arousal, dominance, and desire to smoke. Additionally, participants assessed SEA’s naturalness and integration, and perceived object presence using a 0–10 scale, alongside qualitative comments.
Results: Within-group analysis showed that smokers reported significantly higher ratings for smoking-related objects compared to control objects across valence, arousal, dominance, and desire to smoke (p < 0.001). Conversely, non-smokers rated control objects higher than smoking-related objects in valence and arousal. Between-group analysis confirmed that smokers reported significantly higher responses to smoking-related objects than non-smokers, particularly regarding desire to smoke (p < 0.001). 
Conclusions: The 3D dataset effectively elicited smoking craving and associated emotional and regulatory responses (valence, arousal, and dominance) in smokers. The SEA provided an immersive and ecologically valid experience, supporting its potential utility as a digital tool for smoking cue-exposure interventions.

articles.title: An Individual-Level Paradigm for Research on Deception Cues: An Urgent Proposal
articles.authors: Erik Mac Giolla; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: All psychological theories of deception cues concern explanatory mechanisms at the level of the individual. However, past research on deception cues compares the behavior of truth tellers and liars at the group level. Unless two conditions are met, that the statistical models do not vary (i) across individuals or (ii) across occasions in time, group-level findings cannot accurately describe the behavior of individuals. We show that these conditions are unlikely to hold for deception cues. This means the current group-level research cannot provide a meaningful test of the individual-level mechanisms key to understanding deception cues. In order to draw meaningful conclusions about these individual-level mechanisms, the field needs a wholly different research paradigm, based on repeated measures designs. We outline a proposal for such an individual-level research agenda. Without this development, fundamental questions in deception research will remain unanswered and theories of deception will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Revisiting the Blind Implantation Paradigm: Robustness of False Memory Induction Under Controlled Conditions
articles.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Sarah Viertel; Henry Otgaar; Kristin Jankowsky
articles.abstract: The Blind Implantation paradigm was introduced as a scalable method for inducing false autobiographical memories without human interaction (Otgaar et al., 2022). We conducted a conceptual replication (N = 348) with a sample three times the size of the original, using a multi-target event design and a non-suggestive control group. Results confirm that the procedure reliably induces false beliefs and memories, supporting the reconstructive nature of memory. However, induction rates (12–15% for beliefs; 8.5% for memories) were substantially lower than in the original study. Furthermore, we found no evidence of an imagination effect, likely attributable to low task compliance. Exploratory analyses of written accounts support the validity of the paradigm and the utilized self-report scales. We discuss the implications for the scalability of memory research, emphasizing the need for comprehensive construct validation to assure differentiation of genuine memory distortion from other experimental effects in unmonitored online settings.

articles.title: Foundations of English as a Foreign Language Literacy: Cognitive and Linguistic Contributions to English Reading and Spelling in Young German Learners
articles.authors: Heike Mlakar; Benjamin Goecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This longitudinal study investigated the cognitive and linguistic predictors of English as a foreign language (EFL) literacy among elementary school children in Germany, focusing on reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, reading fluency, and real-word and pseudoword spelling.

Method: A sample of 107 students (53 boys, 54 girls; M_age = 10.52, SD = 0.64; 82 L1 German, 25 with other L1) was assessed at the beginning of Grade 3 on cognitive abilities (phonological awareness, phonological short-term memory, working memory, nonverbal intelligence) and linguistic skills (English vocabulary and grammar). Linear mixed-effects models, including age, gender, and language background as covariates, were used to predict six EFL literacy outcomes at the end of Grade 4, accounting for the nested data structure.

Results: Nonverbal intelligence and phonological awareness were robust predictors of EFL reading comprehension, with L2 vocabulary adding a further contribution. Beyond comprehension, distinct skills predicted distinct outcomes: phonological short-term memory predicted pseudoword reading, L2 receptive grammar and vocabulary predicted real-word spelling, and nonverbal intelligence predicted pseudoword spelling. These additional effects align with theoretical models and offer encouraging initial evidence that merits replication. Reading fluency was not predicted by the variables examined. 

Conclusion: The findings underscore the necessity of fostering vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, and phonological processing, alongside general cognitive skills, in EFL literacy instruction for young learners. Adopting a multidimensional perspective can inform targeted literacy support strategies and offer a better understanding of the knowledge bases underlying early EFL literacy in non-English-speaking contexts.

articles.title: Overall attitudes towards quantum computing are more positive than overall attitudes towards artificial intelligence considering also knowledge levels
articles.authors: Christian Montag; Rostam J. Neuwirth; Magnus Liebherr
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a major topic of public and scientific debate, whereas public perceptions of quantum computing (QC) remain less understood. In the present study, we aimed to understand if people have different views on AI vs. QC, while also asking them about their perceived knowledge levels in these two domains. Further, we investigated the construct of technology self-efficacy to consider how people in general think they can master new technology. 
In N = 475 German speaking participants from the general population (227 females, 248 males) we observed a) that people report on average more positive attitudes towards QC than towards AI, while b) at the same time reporting less knowledge on QC compared to AI. In mediation models, we observed that the link between technology self-efficacy and more positive AI / QC attitudes is mediated by knowledge levels about AI / QC. We also shed light on further mediation models with negative AI / QC attitudes and pessimism aversion in the context of AI / QC as outcomes. 
The present data could be interpreted in a way that the massive global discussions on AI technology might make people less positive towards this general-purpose technology compared to overall QC attitudes, whereas interestingly the reported knowledge levels about QC are lower than those regarding AI. This is noteworthy, as it is discussed that the fusion of QC and AI technology will represent a powerful merger likely leading to a dramatic increase of scientific discovery, an assumption that received moderate support in the present sample.

articles.title: Obsessive Thinking About a Loved One in Romantic Love: Eight Perspectives
articles.authors: Adam Bode; Sandra Langeslag
articles.abstract: Obsessive thinking about a loved one (i.e., constant, involuntary, repetitive thoughts about the loved one) is a defining feature of romantic love yet remains markedly under-researched. This article provides the first review of obsessive thinking about a loved one in romantic love, organising the disparate literature using an "Eight Perspectives" approach spanning evolutionary history, evolutionary functions, development, mechanisms, ecology, cognitions, emotions, and behaviour. We argue that obsessive thinking about a loved one likely emerged by co-opting mother-infant bonding circuitry, appears across cultures and across the lifespan, and may have evolved to promote proximity-seeking and sustained orientation toward a loved one. Contrary to long-standing claims, the mechanisms underlying obsessive thinking in romantic love are unlikely to be shared with obsessive-compulsive disorder. People who are in love think about their loved one for approximately 50% of their waking hours, and this thinking is associated with romantic (but not companionate) love, distraction, proximity-seeking behaviour, and analgesia. Whether such thinking is experienced as bothersome or enjoyable depends less on its frequency than on companionate love and reciprocation. We conclude by identifying priorities for future research across all eight perspectives.

articles.title: Subjective and physiological measures reveal emotionally salient moments in virtual everyday life
articles.authors: Ruhoollah Akhundzadeh; Johanna Hokka; Mikko Sams; Eeva Puumala; Heini Saarimäki
articles.abstract:
Emotions in everyday life are dynamic, context-dependent, and socially embedded, yet most psychophysiological research relies on highly controlled and often artificial laboratory paradigms. This raises questions about whether emotional processes observed under such conditions generalize to naturalistic contexts and how subjective and physiological measures relate in everyday settings.

The present study addresses these challenges by combining ethnographically informed virtual reality (VR) stimuli with multimodal measurement of emotional responses. Participants viewed immersive 360° videos depicting everyday social encounters while electrocardiography, skin conductance, facial electromyography, and gaze patterns were recorded. Following each scenario, participants provided affective ratings across multiple dimensions, including valence, arousal, approach–avoidance, and social connectedness.

Across measures, results revealed systematic but context-dependent divergence between subjective and physiological responses. Associations between modalities were generally weak and selective rather than reflecting consistent one-to-one correspondence. Instead, different measures appeared to capture complementary aspects of emotional processing. Furthermore, relationships between physiological signals and affective ratings varied across events, highlighting the role of contextual and social meaning in shaping emotional responses.

These findings suggest that emotional experience in everyday contexts cannot be reduced to single physiological or subjective indicators but is better understood as a multi-component, context-sensitive process. The results underscore the importance of multimodal approaches and ecologically valid designs. More broadly, they demonstrate the potential of immersive VR as a methodological framework for studying naturalistic emotional experiences while maintaining experimental control.

articles.title: Development, Content Validation, and Preliminary Accessibility Testing of a Workplace Well-Being Assessment Tool for Workers with Intellectual Disabilities
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Pascale Leconte; Marine Peslier; Sophie Posseme; Anne Palanque; Tiphaine Huyghebaert-Zouaghi; Nolwenn Charles; Julio César Alves Da Silva; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract:
Background: Workplace well-being is a critical determinant of job retention for people with intellectual disabilities. Despite its importance, no validated instrument exists to assess this construct among these workers. The objective of the present research was therefore to develop a battery of questionnaire tailored to people with intellectual disabilities in sheltered employment to assess workplace well-being and its associated factors. Furthermore, this study aimed to provide evidence regarding the instrument's content validity and initial evidence of its accessibility for the target population.
Method: In a first study, the content of the developed questionnaire battery was evaluated by an expert committee using the Lynn method. The instrument included four indicators of workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, need for recovery, vigor, job satisfaction), job characteristics (i.e., job demands and job resources), and off-duty recovery (i.e., recovery activities and experiences), variables based on the JD-R model, DISC-R model and recovery theories. In a second study, this validated questionnaire was administered to 29 participants to assess its accessibility.
Results: All 80 items developed received content validation by the expert committee. The pilot study conducted with the target population provided initial evidence of the instrument accessibility.
Conclusion: Further research is needed to test the questionnaire with a larger sample to provide psychometric evidence and additional evidence of its accessibility for workers with intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy beliefs in pro-environmental behavior change
articles.authors: Christina M. Juchem; Karen R.S. Hamann; Susanne Buecker; Lisa Marie Warner; Saskia Baumgardt; Abira Suthakaran; Leonie C. Bandurski; Eva Asselmann
articles.abstract: Efficacy beliefs – individuals’ conviction that their actions can make a meaningful difference – are widely regarded as key psychological drivers of pro-environmental behavior and promising targets for climate interventions. Yet it remains unclear whether changing these beliefs translates into action. We conducted a preregistered systematic review synthesizing longitudinal and interventional evidence (129 studies; N ≈ 65,000) to evaluate whether, and under what conditions, efficacy beliefs promote pro-environmental behavior change. After correcting for publication bias, efficacy interventions showed no meaningful effect on intention and behavior (d = 0.01-0.04), largely because most interventions failed to reliably increase efficacy beliefs. Multi-session interventions showed greater promise, whereas brief, message-based interventions were ineffective in altering pro-environmental action. These findings challenge assumptions about the malleability and behavioral impact of efficacy beliefs and redirect research toward understanding how efficacy beliefs can be durably strengthened and interact with social and structural factors to promote climate action.

articles.title: Whole-brain anatomical and temporal patterns  hypothesized to be evoked during a false-belief fMRI task
articles.authors: Konrad F. Jennicke; Ava Momeni; Maddie Evora; Todd Stephen Woodward
articles.abstract:
Background: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) investigations of theory of 
mind and false-belief processing have been central to cognitive neuroscience for several 
decades. Drawing on previous fMRI studies, we (1) hypothesize that a task-general brain 
mode (DMB) will emerge during the false-belief task, (2) specify its anatomical properties, 
and (3) hypothesize how it will respond, in terms of blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) 
signal changes, to task conditions in a false-belief task.
Task: The false-belief task involved story processing involving either theory of mind or only 
physical properties, resulting in two conditions: (1) Mental, and (2) Physical.
Anatomical: The spatial patterns for Default Mode B (DMB; Lemon, Headlights, Flying 
Seagull, Tripod and Angel Wings) are provided in Figure 1.
Temporal: DMB is predicted to activate during the Mental condition due to engagement of 
theory of mind processes, and to deactivate during the Physical condition. Both are predicted 
to involve a mid-trial peak activation or deactivation. Details are presented in the text below 
and Figure 3.
Analysis: Constrained Principal Component Analysis for fMRI (fMRI-CPCA), an 
application of multivariate multiple regression with a finite impulse response model of the 
task timing, followed by dimensionality reduction, will be used to test these hypotheses.
Conclusions: For the false-belief task, DMB is hypothesized to emerge and show specific 
spatial and temporal characteristics. Although examined within the context of false-belief 
tasks, this mode is not specific to this task. Rather, it is part of a broader set of task-general 
functional brain modes observed across multiple cognitive tasks. This approach may provide 
insight into cognitive processes detectable by fMRI underlying theory of mind.

articles.title: Minimum Cost Psychological Defense: Theoretical Construction and Anti-Fraud Application
articles.authors: Lijie Zhou; Yifan Zhou; Zihuan Pei
articles.abstract: Human decision-making under acute stress reveals a critical paradox in applied social psychology: despite possessing adequate declarative risk knowledge, individuals frequently exhibit a knowing-doing gap when confronting high-pressure digital deception. Traditional interventions demanding substantial cognitive resources often fail when deceivers hijack victims' limited cognitive bandwidth via emotional manipulation. To address this, we propose the Minimum Cost Psychological Defense (M.C.P.D.) model. In Study 1, using a mixed-methods design (N = 679), we developed and validated the Public Anti-Fraud Skill Scale. It comprises three dimensions—emotional buffering, proactive defense, and distributed help-seeking—which significantly predicted reduced real-world victimization risk. In Study 2, a double-blind randomized controlled trial (N = 185) evaluated an emergency guide that encodes complex verification tasks into simple implementation intentions. Compared to traditional education, this micro-skill intervention significantly reduced compliance impulses under simulated high-pressure fraud scenarios and shortened decision-making response times, indicating successful cognitive offloading. By transforming declarative knowledge into procedural, automated micro-skills, the M.C.P.D. strategy effectively bypasses executive function limitations. This shifts the anti-fraud paradigm from trait assessment to dynamic behavioral blocking, providing significant contributions to dual-process theory and a scalable tool for practical interventions.

articles.title: Realistic deepfakes are detected better from a single glance than deliberate inspection
articles.authors: Dalia Israel; Timothy Cottier; Genevieve Quek; Manuel Varlet; Tijl Grootswagers
articles.abstract: The rapidly increasing realism of AI-generated faces threatens trust in digital media, as observers often fail to reliably distinguish AI-generated faces from real faces under prolonged viewing. Across three experiments, participants (N = 300) classified faces varying in realism, exposure duration, and feature availability as real or AI-generated. Observers detected AI-generated faces above chance based on 83 ms when external features, such as hair and background, were present, whereas unlimited viewing did not improve detection of realistic AI-generated faces. These findings suggest observers can extract gist-based authenticity-related signals from a single glimpse, but these may be overridden during prolonged evaluative face processing.

articles.title: Acoustic and social bonding differences between Japanese singing and conversation: A Registered Report replicating Ozaki et al. (2024)
articles.authors: Gakuto Chiba; Yuto Ozaki; Shinya Fujii; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Understanding cross-cultural differences between singing and speech is a central goal of the Many Voices project (Savage et al. 2025a). As part of this effort, the present study examined Japanese participants (n=10 for confirmatory acoustic analysis; 15 for exploratory behavioural analysis) singing the traditional folk song Tokyo Ondo or having a conversation about favourite foods. Confirmatory analyses replicated previously reported tendencies (Ozaki et al., 2024): singing was higher in pitch, slower in temporal rate, and used more stable pitches than spoken conversation. Temporal rate showed a large effect (Cohen’s d = 1.6), while pitch height (d = 0.55) and pitch stability (d = 0.39) showed medium effect sizes. Exploratory analyses of relationships between acoustic features and social variables suggested that singing increased participants’ self-reported sense of social bonding, and individuals reporting higher perceived synchrony tended to show greater singing–speech differences. This study provides culturally grounded data of Japanese conversation and traditional singing for cross-cultural vocal research and underscores the importance of including traditional repertoires in studies of acoustic variation. The Many Voices project will continue collecting data from up to 24 additional languages and regions, with a subsequent meta-analysis assessing cross-linguistic consistency in singing–speech differences.

articles.title: Personality improves prediction of the onset of common mental disorders
articles.authors: Ye Zhang; Michelle Luciano; Uku Vainik; René Mõttus
articles.abstract: Common mental disorders (CMDs) are among the leading causes of disability worldwide, yet identifying who is at risk before clinical presentation remains a central challenge. Personality traits are promising candidates: stable across decades, measurable long before onset, inexpensive to assess and conceptually continuous with psychopathology. Here we test whether personality predicts new-onset CMDs across six ICD-10 categories spanning depressive, anxiety, stress-related, somatoform, and sleep disorders in 63,672 Estonian Biobank adults with linked registry diagnoses, using elastic net models with temporally independent validation in which test cases had been diagnosis-free for at least 17 years before personality assessment. Fine-grained personality nuances (items) predicted incident CMDs over a three-year follow-up with mean AUC = 0.71 (across-disorder range 0.67–0.79), exceeding Big Five domains (0.67) and demographics (0.59). Models trained on one disorder predicted the other five with comparable accuracy, indicating that personality identifies a broadly shared CMD liability, well suited to general risk screening rather than differential diagnosis. With as few as 15–30 items retaining most of this accuracy, brief personality assessment offers a scalable approach for stratifying general CMD risk up to three years before clinical diagnosis.

articles.title: Immediate reward reduces procrastination in a naturalistic multi-day task
articles.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Yijun Lin; Falk Lieder; Wei Ji Ma
articles.abstract: Procrastination is costly and pervasive, and delivering rewards immediately is a widely recommended intervention in self-help advice, yet this advice lacks experimental support. A key challenge in testing it is designing a paradigm that both mimics real-world environments where procrastination arises and permits experimental manipulation. Here we introduce the Multi-day Online Reading Task (MORT), which combines these properties and enables measurement of the full time course of work. In a preregistered experiment (n = 611), participants were given seven days to complete a self-paced reading task and received payment either immediately upon task completion or one day after the deadline. Immediate reward led all participants to start earlier and led those with high trait procrastination, who need help most, to complete work units and the overall task earlier across three reward-performance relationships. The benefits were mediated by motivation and did not come at the cost of task completion or persistence. These findings provide causal evidence that immediate reward reduces procrastination.

articles.title: The Entangled Loop: Emotion, quantum-like interference and hierarchy in the architecture of consciousness
articles.authors: Morten L. Kringelbach; Fernando Rosas; Ruben Eero Laukkonen; Shamil Chandaria; Yonatan Sanz Perl; Gustavo Deco
articles.abstract: We propose three entangled characteristics that explain the functional properties of consciousness: Emotion, quantum-like interference and hierarchy. The argument proceeds from thermodynamic first principles. Biological systems must stay far from equilibrium at minimal energy cost, and emotion is one of evolution’s heuristic solutions to this constraint. Valenced summary statistics compress the intractable decision space of survival into rapidly evaluable approximations. The same thermodynamic pressure selects for greater representational power at lower energy cost by promoting quantum-like inference – through interference in coupled oscillators across spectral gaps in structural connectivity – and hierarchical integration through a core group of orchestrating regions. Here we first derive emotion as the thermodynamic compression of adaptive decision-making and review the direct causal tractability of the distributed hedonic network through deep brain stimulation and optogenetic intervention. Second, we show how quantum-like inference follows from the same thermodynamic pressure demanding hierarchical orchestration, and we distinguish the physical mechanism of interference from the computational function of inference it makes possible. Third, we ask whether emotion is architectural rather than a weighted parameter within an otherwise neutral model. Support comes from recent mechanistic interpretability research on large language models, recovering the three features of two-dimensional geometry of mammalian emotion, quantum-like representations and synergistic hierarchy in human linguistic output. We argue that these signatures are the echo of the consciousness-generating architecture in the language it produces, not evidence that language models are themselves conscious. We draw out some of the consequences of this perspective for theories of consciousness, for the hard problem, for falsifiable empirical prediction and for the clinical restoration of flourishing. This convergent evidence supports our account of the Entangled Loop: A perspective on consciousness in which emotion is architecturally primary, quantum-like inference binds conscious content, and where the orchestrating regions coordinate both. This offers a principled route to rebalancing the affective architecture in neuropsychiatric disorders and to flourishing understood as meaningful pleasure achievable in the moment.

articles.title: A spatiotemporal hierarchy for social interaction perception in the lateral visual stream
articles.authors: Emalie McMahon; Elizabeth Jiwon Im; Michael Bonner; Leyla Isik
articles.abstract: The lateral visual stream has been recently proposed as a third visual stream, in addition to the ventral and dorsal streams, specialized for processing dynamic social content. While prior work has suggested that the regions of this pathway form a hierarchy representing increasingly abstract information, the computations along this pathway are still largely unknown. High spatiotemporal resolution data are particularly informative for characterizing the information flow and thus neural computations across different brain regions. Using a novel regression approach, we combine data from EEG, fMRI, and behavior in response to the same videos to leverage the high temporal resolution of EEG and whole-brain spatial resolution of fMRI. We find that low-level visual features are represented in early visual cortex with a short temporal latency and are not represented in higher-level regions of the lateral stream. Further, we find that mid-level features are represented in mid-level lateral regions with a shorter latency than high-level features in more anterior regions of the lateral pathway. However, both mid- and high-level features were decodable in anterior regions of the lateral pathway with a similar latency. Together, these results provide evidence that features of social actions are processed rapidly in the lateral visual stream in a manner that is consistent with hierarchical processing, but the lateral stream does not exhibit a strict temporal sequence of representational transformations along the posterior-to-anterior axis.

articles.title: Can modifiable dementia risk factors help account for the predictive link between personality and midlife cognitive health? Evidence from a 17-year longitudinal study of Mexican-origin adults
articles.authors: Emorie D Beck; Evan A. Warfel; Winkie Ma; Angelina Sutin; Richard Robins
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Prior research has established that dementia risk factors and personality traits separately predict cognition in mid-to-late life. The present research tests whether Lancet Commission dementia risk factors mediate the link between personality and midlife cognitive function. 
METHODS: We examined whether the latent levels and slopes of Big Five personality trajectories were associated with midlife cognitive function and ten modifiable dementia risk factors (e.g., hypertension, depression symptoms, sleep problems), using data from a 17-year longitudinal study of 1,106 Mexican-origin adults in the United States.
RESULTS: All Big Five domains had prospective associations with multiple dementia risk factors and with cognitive impairment, cognitive function, and self-reported memory. Individuals higher in Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness had lower levels of dementia risk factors, lower likelihood of cognitive impairment, and better cognitive function. Individuals higher in Neuroticism generally showed the opposite pattern. Specific risk factors (depression, hearing loss, and hypertension) mediated the association between personality and some cognitive outcomes.
DISCUSSION: By examining how dementia risk factors relate to personality traits and cognitive health outcomes, we clarify whether modifiable risk factors account for the personality–cognition link in Mexican-origin adults, an underrepresented population at greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.

articles.title: Outcomes of Peer Coaching, Peer Tutoring, and Peer Mentoring Among International Students: A Scoping Review Protocol
articles.authors: Xiaohan Huang; Xi Liu; Lynn Williams
articles.abstract:
Objective: The objective of this scoping review is to map and summarise the existing literature on the outcomes of peer coaching, peer mentoring, and peer tutoring among international students.   

Introduction: International students frequently encounter a combination of academic, psychological, and cultural challenges. Peer coaching, peer mentoring, and peer tutoring offer the potential to provide accessible, culturally responsive, and cost-effective forms of peer support. Despite this potential, existing research on these interventions remains fragmented across diverse contexts including workplace settings, nursing education, and teacher training programmes, and only a small number of studies have focused specifically on international students in higher education. A scoping review is therefore required to systematically map the existing evidence, clarify what is currently known, and identify key gaps to inform future research and practice.

Inclusion criteria: This review will include international students enrolled in higher education institutions. This study will also include peer coaching, peer mentoring, and peer tutoring delivered in any format (e.g., face-to-face, online, one-to-one, or group-based). Eligible evidence will consist of peer-reviewed empirical studies using experimental, quasi-experimental, observational, qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods designs with no restriction on publication date. Only English-language publications will be considered due to feasibility constraints. Studies focusing on non-international populations, non-educational settings, or interventions not involving a peer-based approach will be excluded. 

Methods: This scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The review protocol will be registered on the Open Science Framework. A comprehensive search will be conducted across MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, CINAHL, Embase, and APA PsycINFO to identify studies examining peer coaching, peer mentoring, and peer tutoring among international students in higher education. The search strategy will include both controlled vocabulary and free-text terms, and will be developed in consultation with an academic librarian. Additional studies will be identified through reference list screening of included articles. Eligible studies will be independently screened by two reviewers using a two-stage process (title/abstract and full-text screening), with disagreements resolved through discussion or a third reviewer. Data will be extracted using a standardised data extraction form and synthesised descriptively.

Ethics: As this is a scoping review, it will not require ethical approval as it will synthesise data from publicly available published studies.

articles.title: Insights from Interpretable Machine Learning into the Interplay of Model Misspecifications, Fit Indices, and Nuisance Parameters
articles.authors: Melanie Viola Partsch; Mirka Henninger; Carmen Ximénez Gómez; David Goretzko
articles.abstract:
Researchers routinely evaluate structural equation models using global fit indices such as the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR, often interpreting them against fixed cutoff values. However, these
indices are influenced not only by model misspecifications but also by nuisance parameters including sample size, model complexity, and item reliability, complicating their interpretation. Although previous studies have documented many such effects, their findings remain fragmented. In this study, we integrate existing evidence and explore the potential of Interpretable Machine
Learning (IML) to replicate and extend prior findings. Specifically, we apply feature importance, feature interaction, and two-dimensional accumulated local effects to a machine learning classifier
that distinguishes correctly specified measurement models from differently misspecified models. Overall, the IML approach reproduced several well-established findings while also generating
novel insights, although its ability to recover all previously reported effects was limited. In particular, item reliability features were most important and interacted most strongly with all four
fit indices, replicating known loading-size effects. Furthermore, the results suggested data/model dimensionality as a comparatively unexplored determinant of fit index behavior. These findings
illustrate both the promise and the limitations of IML for synthesizing and extending knowledge about the behavior of global fit indices in structural equation modeling.

articles.title: “Sorting the Good from the mIERda” – Introducing and Testing the performance of the Multidimensional Insufficient Effort Responding Detection Approach (mIERda)
articles.authors: Ariane J. Gauthier; Luc Pelletier; Christopher Gravel
articles.abstract: While the scientific community is increasingly recognizing the relevance of addressing insufficient effort responding (IER) in survey data, the reliance of current IER detection approaches on cut-offs limits their implementation and complexifies the identification, prevalence estimation, and measurement of the impact of IER. The present article illustrates, across four simulation studies, an innovative application of a fair-cut forest algorithm by introducing the multidimensional Insufficient Effort Responding detection approach (mIERda). Built on an unsupervised learning approach, the mIERda was designed to streamline the IER screening process, address methodological gaps associated with current detection approaches, and fit a maximum of survey specifications. In the present article, the discriminative potential of various indicators of IER (Study 1a) and classification accuracy of the mIERda (Study 1b) were assessed and compared to the current gold standard approach across three scales and various settings applied using standard thresholds recommended from the literature. The classification accuracy was then assessed in datasets containing real human data (Study 2) contaminated with simulated IER respondents and when multiple scales are screened at once (Study 3). Overall, we found the mIERda to be more accurate than our application of the gold standard in simulated and human attentive data. The mIERda was also found to have greater levels of balanced accuracy in longer scales and when the severity of IER was higher. The conditions impacting the classification performance of the mIERda are also discussed. Overall, results provide evidence of the criterion validity of the mIERda and position it as an accurate IER detection approach.

articles.title: Lexical Decision with Real and Deepfake-Generated Voice
articles.authors: Lucy Sousa Pereira; Thiago Oliveira Motta Sampaio
articles.abstract: In this study, we applied a lexical decision task to examine whether deepfake-cloned voice processing differs from that of a real voice. Eighty trisyllabic stimuli were selected across five types: low-frequency words (N1), intermediate-frequency words (N2), high-frequency words (N3), pseudowords (PW), and non-words (NW). Word frequency was determined using wordfreq v3.0 and validated against two Brazilian Portuguese corpora in Sketch Engine (PT23 and TLD Brazil); k-means cluster analysis (k = 3; silhouette coefficient M = 0.7063) and PCA (PC1 = 97.3% of variance) yielded three frequency levels, with 16 words selected per cluster by minimum Euclidean distance to the centroid. Pseudowords were generated using the UniPseudo trigram algorithm fed with a Portuguese corpus; non-words were constructed from phonotactically unacceptable onsets filtered by Levenshtein distance (minimum distance ≤ 3 from the 50,000 most frequent words in wordfreq). Real voice recordings were produced in an acoustically treated laboratory (LAPROS/Unicamp) using a HyperX DuoCast microphone in Audacity (wav format); cloned voices were generated in MiniMax Audio (Speech 2.8 HD, Speed 1, Pitch 0, Volume 1), from a profile trained on the research supervisor's voice (second author) with neutralized emotion. Non-words were presented in real voice only, as the cloned voice profile could not render phonotactically unacceptable sound clusters. Twenty-six participants (15 female, 11 male; M age = 30.2 years, SD = 12.0) completed the experiment remotely via Pavlovia, running a PsychoPy (v. 2025.2.3) script using headphones. In each trial, participants pressed S (sim/yes) or N (não/no) to indicate whether the stimulus was a Brazilian Portuguese word; response time was measured from audio onset. A Latin square distributed real and cloned versions (8 each) of each stimulus type across two experiment versions. Reaction times were winsorized using the Outlier Labeling Rule (g = 2.2), and both reaction time and accuracy were modeled with linear mixed-effects models (Python 3.12, statsmodels), including crossed random effects of participant and item, fitted in an interaction model (condition × voice type) and an additive model. Results showed a strong lexical frequency effect: N1 and PW were the slowest conditions (both approximately +0.35 s relative to the overall mean of 0.944 s; p < .001), while N2 and N3 were significantly faster (−0.318 s and −0.392 s; p < .001). Voice type had no significant main effect on reaction time (p = .979) or accuracy (p = .462). The only exception was a PW × Cloned interaction (+0.084 s; p = .016), indicating greater processing cost specifically for pseudowords presented in cloned voice. These findings suggest that listeners process deepfake-cloned voice very similarly to real voice during lexical access, with divergence limited to the pseudoword condition.

articles.title: Culture in psychology and neuroscience: Concepts, relevance, and empirical evidence in rhythm perception
articles.authors: Rainer Polak; Anne Danielsen; Nori Jacoby; Lara Pearson; Samuel Horlor; Stéphane Aubinet; Justin London; Sylvie Nozaradan
articles.abstract: Perceptual systems adapt through individual experience across the lifespan, an ability referred to as plasticity. To understand perceptual plasticity, a promising avenue is to investigate how perception is shaped by cultural experience, as a process deeply embedded within collective practices of cultural production and social learning. The current review synthesizes findings from recent behavioral experiments investigating cross-cultural variation in rhythm perception. Specifically, these studies show that fundamental perceptual processes, such as event timing and rhythm categorization, display shared features but also systematic differences across cultural groups. Critically, these differences correlate with statistically prominent and socially relevant features of cultural production, revealing how perceptual systems are tuned to their music-cultural environments. Yet, how can cross-cultural differences in perception be related back to the collective practices that produce the diversity of cultural environments in the first place? To bridge this gap, we propose perceptual niche construction as an evolutionary approach that positions culture as both a source and a product of perceptual plasticity. That is, cultural experience tunes individual perception, yielding culturally diverse perceptual processes. These processes, in turn, create selection pressures shaping cultural production across nested timescales, resulting in diverse cultural environments. This approach presents implications for research in psychology and neuroscience, notably in proposing to operationalize culture as communities of learning and practice. Moreover, it highlights the relevance of contextually situated research, in view of accounting for the dynamic nature of culture-driven perceptual plasticity.

articles.title: Attractor Accommodation: A Minimal Network  Model of Plasticity-Driven Persistence After Focal  Fixation
articles.authors: Muhammed Joghatayi
articles.abstract:
This study examines whether a configuration held by focal external constraint can become 
internally supported through bounded Hebbian-like plasticity. We address this question in a 
minimal Hopfield network motivated by delusional encapsulation, where a fixed belief-like 
element may persist within an otherwise functional cognitive system.
We introduce attractor accommodation, an attractor-network account of plasticity-driven 
persistence: when a belief-like element is held fixed, Hebbian-like plasticity reorganizes 
surrounding connections so that configurations incorporating it become lower-energy states.
We implemented this in a Hopfield network with one clamped node and bounded Hebbian-like 
plasticity and report three findings. (1) Bounded plasticity creates persistent post-clamp fixation, 
with a sharp threshold (ηcritical≈0.008 at α=100) above which all seeds remain trapped. (2) A 
weight-swap control isolates persistence to the plastic weight matrix: from the same 
accommodated state, the original matrix produced 100% recovery, the plastic matrix 0% (n=30). 
(3) The accommodated basin's resistance to perturbation scales with η×α, and the weight changes 
building it spare high-connectivity nodes (r=−0.80); the state remains a single-node (1−2/N) 
deviation across N∈{50,100,200}. Findings replicated under weight-decay normalization and 
generalized across loads (P/N=0.06–0.14); recovery depended more on accommodation depth 
and sustained focal duration than on perturbation structure.
The model identifies a minimal mechanism by which a transiently imposed focal configuration 
becomes embedded in the weight matrix and persists after release. Hypothesis-generating rather 
than clinically validating, it offers a formal account of delusional encapsulation: persistence may 
reflect not only the focal content but also the accommodation of the surrounding network.

articles.title: Who Gets and Gives the Benefit of the Doubt? Speaker Accent and Listener Background in the Noisy-Channel Framework
articles.authors: Tyler Call; Anna Cole; Olessia Jouravlev
articles.abstract: Language comprehension often requires listeners to infer a speaker’s intended meaning when the literal input is implausible. Within a noisy-channel framework, a foreign accent may signal greater production-related noise, encouraging listeners to reinterpret anomalous utterances rather than accept them literally. The present study replicated and extended the foreign-accent benefit by testing whether listeners’ language backgrounds shape non-literal interpretation (NLI). Across two online experiments, participants heard semantically implausible English sentences (e.g., double-object constructions with reversed thematic roles) produced in either a native or foreign accent and answered comprehension questions indexing literal versus plausible interpretations. Experiment 1 compared monolingual and multilingual native English listeners. Foreign-accented speech elicited more NLIs than native-accented speech, and this accent effect was larger among multilinguals, suggesting that multilingual experience increases sensitivity to accent as a cue to communicative noise. Experiment 2 compared multilingual listeners with English as an L1 or L2. L2 English listeners produced more NLIs overall than L1 English listeners, but the foreign-accent benefit was comparable across groups. These findings indicate that listener language background influences noisy-channel comprehension in distinct ways: multilingualism sharpens accent-based adjustment of noise priors, whereas processing in an L2 raises the baseline tendency to infer plausible intended meanings during comprehension.

articles.title: Brain age gap, cortisol reactivity, and developmental timing of childhood maltreatment in major depressive disorder
articles.authors: Rotem Dan; Sarah Syed; Lauren M. Hutson; Aliza Brown; Emma Holly Palermo; Emily Belleau; Roselinde Kaiser; Fei Du; Diego A. Pizzagalli
articles.abstract:
Objective: Major depressive disorder (MDD), childhood maltreatment, and physiological stress responsivity have each been linked to accelerated biological aging, yet how they jointly relate to brain age gap remains unclear. This study investigated whether brain age gap is associated with depression status and severity, the developmental timing and severity of childhood sexual abuse, and cortisol reactivity.
Methods: Two independent samples of women (Study 1: N=71; Study 2: N=85) included participants with current MDD, remitted MDD, or healthy controls, with childhood sexual abuse histories. Childhood sexual abuse occurred during ages 5–14 years in Study 1 and 11–18 years in Study 2. Brain age gap was estimated from structural MRI using a machine-learning framework. Associations of brain age gap with maltreatment severity, depression severity, and cortisol responses to acute stress (Study 2) were examined.
Results: Brain age gap was associated with childhood maltreatment only among women with current MDD. The direction of association differed according to the developmental timing of childhood sexual abuse, with negative associations following early exposure and positive associations following later exposure. Conversely, brain age gap was related to depression severity only among women without maltreatment histories. Women with current MDD and childhood sexual abuse showed increased cortisol responses to acute stress relative to other groups, and cortisol reactivity exhibited group-dependent nonlinear associations with brain age gap. 
Conclusions: Brain age gap reflects individual differences related to depression status, childhood maltreatment, and cortisol responsivity. These findings highlight brain age gap as a potential indicator of heterogeneity within depression.

articles.title: Recommendations for Recruiting Clinically-Relevant Stratified Samples Across Race/Ethnicity, Gender, and Socioeconomic Status Using the Prolific Online Platform
articles.authors: Julia Machina; Kimberly A. Muellers; Xiqiao Chen; E. Samuel Winer
articles.abstract: Though online sampling methods have progressed, psychology literature continues to include primarily white, educated, upper-class samples. This work will outline the methodology of a stratified community study examining demographic differences in fear of happiness and depression among U.S. adults. Drawing on prior research suggesting variation in emotional processes across social identities, we implemented a fully crossed stratified sampling design to ensure equal representation across race/ethnicity (Black, Asian, Latine, White), gender (cisgender male, cisgender female), and socioeconomic status (SES). Eligible participants were 18-65 years old and residing in the U.S. SES categories were defined as ≤ $50,000 (low), $50,000 - $100,000 (middle), and ≥ $100,000 (high). A priori power analysis (G*Power) indicated a target of 42 participants per cell (N=1,008) to detect medium effects. Following the exclusion of 75 uncategorizable cases, the per-cell target was adjusted to 38, maintaining adequate power for medium-to-large effects. Participants were recruited in SES-based blocks via Prolific. Procedures to preserve stratification, confidentiality, and analytic rigor will be discussed, highlighting methodological considerations for equity-focused psychological research. These methods can ensure adequate power and representation when examining relationships between intersectional identities and psychological phenomena in online samples.

articles.title: Period and Prejudice: Cultural Differences in Menstrual Health between South Asian and White British Women
articles.authors: Michèle Denise Birtel; Lucia Volpi; Aisha Mirza; Laura M König
articles.abstract:
Background: Attitudes towards menstruation are shaped by cultural and social norms and can result in misperceptions, impacting women’s health. Yet, research on cultural differences in menstrual health remains limited. 
Objectives: This study aimed to examine whether South Asian and White British women living in the UK differ in menstrual health, with a focus on menstrual experiences, menstrual literacy, stigma-related factors, and ethnic microaggressions in the healthcare context. 
Design: White British (n = 153) and South Asian (n = 153) menstruating women living in the UK participated in a preregistered cross-sectional online survey. 
Methods: Menstrual experiences were assessed via menstrual distress, symptom management, and hygiene behaviors. Menstrual stigma was measured through affective internalized stigma, internalized stigma of seeking help, secrecy, and avoidance behaviors. 
Results: In addition to differences in menstrual experiences (menstrual pain, symptom management, hygiene behaviors), South Asian women reported lower menstrual literacy than White British women. South Asians also reported greater secrecy as well as stronger avoidance behaviors related to discussing menstruation and engaging in daily activities while menstruating, but also more positive emotions towards menstruation. Additionally, they experienced more ethnic microaggressions in healthcare. Secrecy and microaggressions mediated the effect of ethnic group on self-stigma of seeking help. 
Conclusion: Our findings suggest cultural differences in menstrual health, emphasizing the need for inclusive health education and stigma-reduction interventions. Addressing menstrual literacy gaps, and tackling stigma in family and microaggressions in healthcare settings may improve support for South Asian women in the UK.

articles.title: Thought experiments elicit non-emotional intuitions that motivate altruistic behavior
articles.authors: Celso Vieira
articles.abstract: Philosophers and scientists have long used thought experiments (TEs) to elicit intuitive judgments that prove a point in a rational discussion. This study tests whether TEs can elicit non-emotional intuitions that motivate charitable giving. To accomplish this, the study compares the effectiveness of emotional testimonials and argumentative thought experiments in encouraging altruistic behavior. The valence dimension is also tested. One testimonial evokes positive feelings (inspiration), while the other evokes negative feelings (guilt). One TE is based on the positive duty to help, while the other relies on the negative duty to avoid harming others. Self-reported feelings are also measured. Additionally, the TEs design is distinctive. They present a clear, stepwise, argumentative structure of analogical reasoning. Moreover, TEs are interactive, allowing participants to express their agreement or disagreement at each step. This interaction permits a fine-grained measurement of agreement and reduces the likelihood that participants will feel manipulated. The TE for a positive duty to help others was particularly effective, even when controlling for the mediation of emotions. The detection of non-emotional, rational intuition adds to the body of research suggesting that the dichotomy of intuition/emotion versus deliberation/reflection is too simplistic to capture human decision-making and action processes.

articles.title: Non-conscious knowledge of complex regularities supports instrumental conditioning: A registered report
articles.authors: Răzvan Jurchiș; Andrei Preda; Andrei Razvan Costea; Lina Skora
articles.abstract: Instrumental conditioning (IC) consists in actively learning to approach rewarding stimuli and to avoid punishing stimuli. This central process for adaptation requires a relatively high computational capacity because it entails the integration of knowledge regarding stimuli, behaviours, and outcomes. Recent studies using subliminal exposure show that IC occurs only for consciously perceived stimuli, suggesting that IC may require awareness. In the present study, we investigated whether IC could occur when implicit processing is stimulated not by subliminal exposure but by employing predictive regularities that are complex and difficult to detect consciously. In a novel IC task based on the artificial grammar learning task, participants gave approach (Go) or avoidance responses (No-Go) to strings from two grammars. Unbeknown to them, one of the grammars was reward-predictive and the other was punishment-predictive. Trial-by-trial measures assessed participants’ awareness of the grammar structures and of their judgments regarding the predictive value of the strings. In both an IC phase and a delayed responding phase, we found that participants responded adaptively when they were aware of the regularities and, also, when they were not. Importantly, we found reliable evidence that non-conscious regularities produced adaptive responding only when they produced conscious judgments regarding the predictive values of the stimuli. When judgment knowledge was unconscious, data were insensitive or more consistent with chance performance. This suggests that IC may be produced by a combination of unconscious learning and conscious integration.

articles.title: Identifying Signal in the Noise: A Systematic Review of Resting State fMRI after Traumatic Brain Injury
articles.authors: Emily L. Dennis; Mary R Newsome; Hannah Michelle Lindsey; Nicola L. de Souza; Adrian I. Onicas; Finian Keleher; Courtney McCabe; Charles Rey; C. Lexi Baird; Hollie Mullen
articles.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) has become a widely-deployed methodology in human neuroscience, and its application to traumatic brain injury (TBI) has produced a rapidly growing literature. Efforts to synthesize this literature are complicated by methodological heterogeneity, including differences in data cleaning, denoising, and, critically, brain parcellation, leaving the field without consensus regarding the network response to brain injury. injury. We conducted a systematic review of 219 rsfMRI studies spanning the full TBI spectrum: civilian mild TBI, sports-related head impacts, military TBI, pediatric TBI, moderate-to-severe TBI, and intimate partner violence-related brain injury. All findings are remapped to a common network atlas (Seitzman) and organized by patient population, injury phase, and network. Our primary observation is that much of the apparent inconsistency reflects meaningful variability rather than noise. Coherent patterns emerge when findings are organized this way: within-network hypoconnectivity predominates acutely in civilian mTBI, sports-related concussion shows the opposite pattern of early within-network hyperconnectivity, moderate-to-severe TBI follows a protracted trajectory from early hypoconnectivity through compensatory hyperconnectivity toward eventual normalization or permanent disconnection, and pediatric findings are shaped by sex, symptom status, and developmental stage. Across populations, the default mode and frontoparietal networks show the most consistent alterations, and graph theory studies provide a coherent temporal framework. Methodological factors, including motion mitigation (e.g., global signal regression) and analytic approach, account for a substantial portion of between-study divergence. This review concludes that rsfMRI is a viable approach for modeling systems-level plasticity after TBI and identifies key methodological priorities for the field moving forward.

articles.title: Adopting a Creative Persona: Effects of Perspective-Priming on Creativity and Question-Asking
articles.authors: Ilana Shinder; Tuval Raz
articles.abstract: Creativity supports abilities such as innovation, learning, and artistic production, but people often treat their own creative ability as relatively fixed. The present preregistered experiment tested whether briefly adopting the perspective of someone described as creative is associated with changes in creative abilities such as divergent-thinking and question-asking performance. Participants (N = 201) completed divergent-thinking and question-asking tasks before and after reading a vignette about a target person named Alex, who was described as having either a highly creative or non-creative personality. In the post-prime phase, participants completed the tasks from Alex's perspective. We find that compared with the non-creative-prime group, the creative-prime group produced more fluent and more creative responses on the divergent thinking task, and these effects remained after controlling for baseline performance. The creative-prime group also produced more questions, but their questions were rated as less creative and did not differ in complexity. Across participants, some post-prime outcomes improved relative to baseline, whereas question fluency and creativity decreased. These findings suggest that creative perspective taking may enhance some forms of divergent thinking, while also highlighting its limits for improving creative question quality. Ultimately, these results imply that individuals can temporarily unlock certain creative capacities through simple cognitive reframing, demonstrating that creative potential is more malleable than commonly believed.

articles.title: Intervention-Induced Neuroticism Change Across Multiple Timescales
articles.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Neuroticism is one of the most consequential personality traits for individuals and society. Interventions that facilitate changes in this trait may thus have far-reaching benefits, with initial evidence supporting that interventions can foster lasting neuroticism change. Most personality theories posit that changes in broad, enduring traits are mediated via lower-level changes in momentary states and intermediary habits. However, there are few direct tests of this theorized bottom-up pathway, leaving the mechanisms, direction, and timing of effects unclear. Using data from the Changing How I Live Life Study (N = 444), which evaluated a digital intervention to reduce neuroticism, we examined 1) the shape and magnitude of intervention-induced neuroticism change across three timescales, 2) concurrent and lagged associations among these changes, and 3) whether these associations varied across treatment groups receiving strategies targeting different neuroticism levels. We found that neuroticism changed nonlinearly across the intervention; changes in momentary, daily, and weekly neuroticism measures reliably predicted one another, with bottom-up effects often being larger in magnitude; and mean-level changes and coupled changes in momentary, daily, and weekly neuroticism measures were larger in the intervention groups than in the active control group. These results support the conceptual and causal importance of both bottom-up and top-down (momentary, specific ⟷ long-term, broad) change processes. Together, this study tested key theoretical predictions about the process and directionality of intervention-induced personality change to help elucidate mechanisms underlying intentional personality changes and generate insights about how to enhance intervention efficacy.

articles.title: Milestones in the Wild: Mapping Early Gross Motor Development With the Pebbles App
articles.authors: Lisa Wagner; Flavia Jessica Pfister; Miriam Teresa Löffler; Salome Wenk; Moritz M. Daum
articles.abstract:
Understanding infant development requires methods that capture behaviour as it unfolds in everyday life rather than only in laboratory settings. In a sample of N=
6,755 children (N = 6,046 caregivers), we used caregiver-reported data to examine the emergence of gross motor skills across the first two years. Data was collected using the Pebbles App, a multilingual smartphone app that allows caregivers to document children’s developmental milestones in daily life. We analysed the age of attainment for 60 gross motor milestones using censored event-time methods that incorporated exact, interval-censored, left-censored, and right-censored observations. We then characterised developmental organisation by estimating pairwise ordering probabilities and recurrent milestone sequences. Results showed that ages of attainment spanned a broad developmental range, from early postural and rolling skills in the first months of life to more advanced locomotor and balance skills towards the end of the second year. Estimates generated by the Pebbles App data were broadly consistent with international reference windows for overlapping milestones, supporting the ecological plausibility of app-based caregiver reports. Pairwise ordering analyses further indicated that sitting unsupported almost always preceded standing unsupported and walking independently, while sitting unsupported and crawling were almost equally likely to precede each other. Together, these findings suggest that app-based caregiver reports can be used not only to estimate when gross motor milestones are attained, but also to describe how developmental pathways are organised in everyday life.

articles.title: Goals remap values and not choices
articles.authors: Kathy Shi; Joseph Heffner; Robb Rutledge
articles.abstract: The ability to pursue different goals is fundamental to adaptive decision-making, yet the mechanisms driving this capacity remain unclear. Decision-making is often thought of as having distinct valuation and choice stages. Goals could potentially act at either stage by remapping values or by remapping choices. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants completed an economic decision-making task choosing between a risky and a safe option under opposing goals to maximize or minimize points. If goals remap choices, people will simply switch to the opposite option under opposing goals. If goals remap values, people will treat losses like gains under opposing goals, leading to only sometimes switching to the opposite option. Across four studies (N=1096) and a preregistered replication (N=500), participant choices were best explained by goals remapping values. Computational modeling based on prospect theory confirmed two counterintuitive predictions of goals remapping value: first, that loss aversion acts on gains under the minimize goal, and second, that individuals systematically make identical choices despite opposing goals due to how they value options. We also found reduced overall outcome sensitivity under the novel minimize goal as measured both by choices and by happiness ratings collected periodically throughout the task. When goal changes were frequent, reduced affective outcome sensitivity predicted reduced choice outcome sensitivity, suggesting that emotional alignment across goals supports rational choice. Together, these findings reveal how goals change values, capturing the behavioral and emotional signatures of goal-directed decision-making.

articles.title: Lost in aggregation: from score-based to representational mentalization
articles.authors: Serena Maria Stagnitto; Celia Martínez Tomás; Serena Lecce; José Antonio Hinojosa; Daniele Gatti
articles.abstract:
Psychological measures are commonly reduced to aggregate scores, such as questionnaire totals, accuracy scores, or human-annotated measures. Although useful, these scores may hide information about the configuration of participants’ responses. The present study took mentalization (i.e., the ability to infer others’ mental states) as a working example to investigate how this domain can be characterized through vector-based response representations in addition to classical scoring. One hundred and sixty-four university participants completed the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), and the Triangles task. For each task, we constructed participant-by-participant distance matrices based on classical scores and on vector representations: IRI item-response profiles, RMET response-choice patterns, and sentence embeddings of open-ended Triangles ToM descriptions. Classical score correlations showed limited convergence across tasks, with only RMET accuracy and Triangles score showing a small positive association. Representational similarity analyses showed that vector-based representations reliably converged with classical score distances within each task, although the associations were modest. Cross-task analyses further indicated that score-based and vector-based representations produced partly different prediction patterns. Overall, these findings suggest that classical mentalization measures organize individual differences differently depending on whether responses are represented as aggregate scores or full response configurations, with implications for how psychologists conceptualize and validate social-cognitive assessment.
Keywords: mentalization; representational similarity analysis; individual differences.

articles.title: Perspectives et connaissances des mondes professionnels : un cours de carrière développant les compétences de hasard planifié
articles.authors: Boris Vallée; Eva Louvet; Séverine Bagot-Renault; Charly Marie; Jean-Félix Hamel
articles.abstract:
#### FRENCH 
Selon la Théorie du Hasard Planifié, les événements imprévus dans les trajectoires professionnelles sont autant d’opportunités de carrières. Les individus gagneraient donc à être réceptifs aux événements imprévus, sinon même à les générer. Dans cette continuité, les conseillers d’insertion et d’orientation pourraient accompagner les individus à développer des compétences de hasard planifié (curiosité, persévérance, flexibilité, optimisme et prise de risque) leur permettant de reconnaître les possibilités offertes par le hasard, d’adopter des comportements propices à en engendrer davantage, et de transformer ces événements imprévus en opportunités de carrières.
