Nous créons, déployons et évaluons les effets d’un cours de carrière favorisant le développement de ces compétences de hasard planifié auprès de 214 étudiant·es en Licence 2 de psychologie de l’Université de Rouen Normandie. L’évaluation pré-post (janvier à avril-mai) montre une amélioration des cinq compétences de hasard planifié, et suggère un rapport plus clair et optimiste quant à leurs futures opportunités académiques et professionnelles. Une analyse en cluster montre que les effets de l’intervention sont d’autant plus positifs que le niveau de compétences de hasard planifié pré-intervention est faible. 

---

#### ENGLISH
According to the Planned Happenstance Theory, unexpected events in career paths are opportunities for career development. Individuals would therefore benefit from being open to unforeseen events, or even actively creating them. Building on this, career and guidance counselors could support individuals in developing planned happenstance skills (curiosity, perseverance, flexibility, optimism, and risk-taking). These skills enable them to recognize opportunities presented by chance, adopt behaviors that may generate such opportunities, and transform unexpected events into career prospects. We designed, implemented, and evaluated the effects of a career course aimed at fostering these planned happenstance skills among 214 second-year psychology students at the University of Rouen Normandy. A pre-post assessment (from January to April-May) revealed improvements in all five planned happenstance skills, and suggests students developed a clearer and more optimistic vision of future educational and professional opportunities. Cluster analysis further showed that the intervention’s positive effects were most pronounced among students with lower pre-intervention levels of planned happenstance skills.

articles.title: Intercorrelations of Paraphilic Interests in a General Population and a Pedophilic Subsample
articles.authors: Emma Neofotistos; Susanna Karlkvist; Pelin Yilmaz; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: Previous studies have found positive associations between a wide range of paraphilic interests, but recent research on a sample of users of child sexual abuse material suggested that pedophilic interest may be unrelated to other paraphilic interests. In the present study, we investigate the intercorrelation of paraphilic interests in a representative sample of the general population of the United States. Network analysis indicated that paraphilic interests, including pedophilic interests, were positively associated with each other and could be meaningfully grouped based on consent.  However, when examining a subsample of people exhibiting at least some pedophilic interest, the association between pedophilic interest and other paraphilias was substantially weaker. Further research with specially recruited populations will be necessary to explain this phenomenon, but we speculate that this observed difference between the full sample and pedophilic subsample may be explained by a related third variable (e.g., hypersexuality).

articles.title: The social ecology of development: The changing structure of preschoolers’ everyday experiences
articles.authors: Nele-Pauline Suffo; Anas Suffo; Pierre-Etienne Martin; Yujin Kim; Anam Zahra; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Everyday social interactions shape human psychological development. Research, however, has primarily relied on controlled settings or brief observations; consequently, the nature of naturalistic everyday experiences remains largely unstudied. To address this gap, we developed an automated multimodal processing pipeline to analyze a large egocentric corpus of naturalistic everyday experiences from 107 children aged three to five years in Germany (267.52 hours). The pipeline detects faces, persons, proximity, and speech types to classify time into interacting, available, or alone states. Results indicate a significant ecological reorganization: social interaction dominates at age three and declines towards a more even distribution between states at age six. Conversational agency remains stable throughout preschool, with children sharing it nearly equally with conversational partners. Crucially, social interactions change in their structure in that isolated social cues become significantly less predictive of interactions with age. Thus, preschool social interactions become less frequent but more diverse with development.

articles.title: Frequency and perceived plasticity of climate-relevant consumer behaviors as a function of physical and social factors
articles.authors: Kristian Steensen Nielsen; Cameron Brick; Wencke Gwozdz; Wilhelm Hofmann; Sander van der Linden; Charlotte Anna Kukowski
articles.abstract: Large-scale changes in consumption are essential for mitigating climate change. Yet, people’s behaviors and their perceptions of what is feasible to change are deeply influenced by their social and physical environments. Despite growing recognition of these influences, empirical evidence integrating both current behavior and perceived feasibility of change remains limited. In this study, we examine the relationship between perceptions of physical and social environments and both the frequency of high-impact transport and food behaviors, as well as their perceived behavioral plasticity—the perceived likelihood of changing such behaviors while considering associated costs and barriers. In exploratory analyses, we also examine how perceived behavioral plasticity relates to perceived wellbeing impacts of behavior change. Using survey data from 1,202 UK adults, we analyzed current driving, air travel, public transport use, and red and white meat consumption, together with perceived plasticity and wellbeing impact for each behavior. Social environmental factors, particularly descriptive norms and family goal support, predicted most current behaviors and perceived plasticity across domains. By contrast, perceptions of physical environmental factors, such as public transport access or food appeal, were associated with behavior and plasticity in more domain-specific ways. Perceived behavioral plasticity was positively correlated with perceived wellbeing impacts, suggesting that perceptions of feasibility and desirability are intertwined. These findings together demonstrate the importance of targeting both physical opportunity structures and social contexts when promoting climate-relevant behavior change.

articles.title: When Felt States Become Social Evidence: An Identifiability Framework for Hot-State Social Inference
articles.authors: Iliana Samara
articles.abstract: People often treat their feelings as evidence about what another person means or intends, but the same judgment shift can reflect valid cue use, response threshold, projection, attentional amplification, or self-state use. This article develops hot-state evidentiary admission theory (HEAT), a middle-range framework for ambiguous, action-relevant social-state inference. HEAT specifies when a self-state becomes target evidence: when it is bodily salient, encounter-plausible, and poorly differentiated from target and context. Its key prediction is source-sensitive cue reweighting. When a self-state is admitted, the self-state and state-consistent global cues should gain weight, ambiguous diagnostic cues should lose weight, and clear diagnostic cues should retain or regain influence under correction. HEAT separates mean shifts from cue utilization and reframes debates in sexual misperception by specifying when feelings function as useful evidence, misleading evidence, or neither.

articles.title: People have an accurate folk theory of conspiracy believers
articles.authors: Marius Mercier; Noëmon Baudouin; Hugo Mercier
articles.abstract: Seeing someone endorse a conspiracy theory could be informative of which other conspiracy theories they might endorse and reveal broader personality traits. Across three pre-registered experiments (N = 775 US participants), we show that these inferences are supported by the nested structure of conspiracy beliefs: individuals who endorse less popular theories tend to endorse more popular ones, but not vice versa. This pattern holds for real-world conspiracy theories (false and true) as well as for invented ones. When presented with the information that someone endorses or rejects a conspiracy theory, participants could predict which other theories that individual would endorse or reject. Moreover, participants could infer the personality traits of conspiracy believers (e.g., narcissism, manichaeism) by appropriately weighing the rarity of the endorsed conspiracy theory. These findings suggest that people use a folk theory of latent conspiracism to draw broadly accurate inferences about conspiracy believers (or non-believers) from limited information.

articles.title: Traditional progressive tests with stopping rules from Computerized Adaptive Testing: Do potential advantages outweigh added complexity?
articles.authors: Jianan Chen; Johan Braeken
articles.abstract: Progressive tests, where items are administered in order of increasing difficulty and test administration is stopped after the respondent has made a prespecified number of errors, are commonplace in psychological and educational practice. The Wechsler intelligence test batteries consist, for instance, of subtests that are based upon this classical adaptive testing format. Stopping a progressive test once frequent errors start to occur makes intuitive sense as the test would, by construction, only get more difficult. Yet, it is unclear how a stopping rule in terms of the number of errors translates into the desired measurement precision and accuracy, and it remains questionable whether stopping everyone after the same number of errors is warranted. In contrast, in modern computerized adaptive testing (CAT), tests are stopped on an individual basis as a function of measurement precision and/or accuracy. In this study, we assess the suitability of three popular CAT-based stopping rules (Change-in-Point-Estimate, Fixed-Precision, and Precision-Gain rules) for use in progressive tests and compare their performance to traditional consecutive-errors stopping rules. The extent to which CAT-based stopping rules can be translated into the simple but transparent count-of-errors metric of traditional stopping rules was explored. Results are discussed from the perspective of the differences in design and test adaptivity between progressive tests and CATs. We conclude with general considerations and implications for optimizing stopping strategies in progressive tests.

articles.title: Digital exposures and adolescent mental health
articles.authors: Sarah Bauermeister; Abhaya Adlakha; Julian Turner; Emma Squires; Simon Thompson; Ian Thompson; Natalie Coles; Ryan D Parsons; Galit Geulayov; John Gallacher
articles.abstract:
Adolescence is characterised by rapid cognitive change representing a substantial increase in cognitive complexity and processing load. The transition to a digital society has further increased complexity and load, providing an explanation for increased levels of poor mental health in young people. 
The impact of social media platform use on mental health was investigated in a sample of 15,135 young people aged 16-19 years from 51 schools, across 31 UK Local Education Authorities, as part of the BrainWaves cohort.
Social media use (hours per day) was marginally greater for girls (x̄ =4.1) than boys (x̄ =3.8). Of the 15 platforms investigated, 12 were related to duration of use (hours per day) in girls and 10 platforms in boys. The platform most strongly related to duration was TikTok (bgirls=1.34, bboys=0.97). 
Duration was associated with poor mental health (higher anxiety and depression scores) in both girls (b=0.29, p<0.001) and boys b=0.35, p<0.001). Non-duration-related platform-specific associations were also found.
Whilst these data do not support a total social media ban for young people, they strengthen the case for limiting access, requiring platform design to promote emotional, cognitive and physical wellbeing, and educating young people to be better informed about social media use.

articles.title: Integrating gaze into models for multi-attribute pricing
articles.authors: Yiming Wang; Anderson K. Fitch; Konstantina Sokratous; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: To assess subjective value and form different types of judgments, people dynamically allocate attention to different attributes of their available options. Despite the development of models that characterize how people dynamically allocation attention during choice, the role of attention in producing other judgments, like pricing, is not well understood. Consequently, it is difficult to explain why they often result in differing apparent preferences. To address this, we measured attention during a multi-attribute pricing task where participants assigned willingness-to-pay prices to stimuli consisting of payoffs, delays, and probabilities, and during a multi-attribute choice task where participants chose between such options from the same stimulus set. Participants showed a strong preference for looking at the payoff attribute first in the pricing task, while the choice task resulted in attribute-wise comparisons that are not possible in pricing paradigms. To account for this behavior during multi-attribute pricing, we developed a model that first anchors on a payoff, and then adjusts to a final price based on information that is accumulated while attending to corresponding attributes. Empirical and modeling results taken together indicated that early anchoring (initial fixations on payoff) as well as architectural differences in information search (within-option vs between-option) produce the observed patterns of preference reversals, necessitating unique attention dynamics and models for choice and pricing tasks.

articles.title: Perceived error climate in primary school classrooms: A multidimensional perspective
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: The way teachers address errors in the classroom plays a crucial role in shaping how students experience their errors, regulate their learning processes, and ultimately learn from them. To capture these dynamics, the concept of the perceived error climate has been introduced, describing the extent to which errors are positively perceived and treated as constructive learning opportunities by teachers and students. Prior research with secondary school students conceptualized the error climate as comprising eight subdimensions organized under a single higher-order factor (Steuer et al., 2013). However, this structure has not yet been confirmed in younger students, and a single second-order factor may not provide a sufficiently differentiated representation of the construct. To address these deficits, we examined the structure of the perceived error climate in primary school classrooms and proposed a novel second-order structure distinguishing between emotional and instructional support following errors. The study drew on a sample of N = 2,628 third- and fourth-grade students from 187 classrooms across two domains (maths and German as a first language). Using multilevel multigroup confirmatory factor analyses, we examined the structure of the perceived error climate at both the individual and the classroom level. Results supported the proposed structure of eight subdimensions loading onto the two second-order factors of emotional and instructional support following errors. These second-order factors were positively related to students’ individual adaptive affective-motivational and adaptive action-related reactions to errors, respectively. Overall, the findings demonstrate that primary school students already perceive the error climate as a multifaceted classroom feature and that these distinctions are relevant for students’ engagement with their own errors.

articles.title: Intertwining experience and evidence: how can co-created causal diagrams guide meaningful research questions about psychosocial processes in pain? A participatory co-design study
articles.authors: Rebecca M. Pearson; Amanda Ly; Neil Heydon-Dumbleton; Alexandria Andrayas; Megan Anne Chambers; Noureen Shivji; Rachael Gooberman-Hill; Samantha Stone; Matthew Nunes; Laura Oporto Lisboa
articles.abstract:
Objectives: To develop and implement a co-creation process for common language and multi-stakeholder engagement to produce a shared causal framework that helps identify meaningful research questions in the context of psychosocial processes in pain and guide data modelling decisions.
Design: Participatory co-design study using facilitated workshops and iterative synthesis to develop a ‘Dream’ Directed Acyclic Graph (Dream-DAG). The Dream-DAG represented an idealised visual causal map unconstrained by available study measures or specific dataset limitations. We used a storm metaphor where different components of the storm (i.e., thunder or lightning) mirror the temporal and causal inference features in DAGs (i.e., exposure or confounding).
Setting: A UK-based multidisciplinary pain research consortium involving researchers, clinicians and public contributors.
Participants: 12 participants took part, including 4 experts by experience living with chronic pain and 8 professionals including a wide range of researchers (from quantitative and qualitative fields), clinicians and data scientists. Participants were invited because of their lived, clinical, methodological or data-related expertise relevant to psychosocial processes in pain.
Results: Through the workshops we developed a shared language for causal thinking, a co-created Dream-DAG, and an operationalised set of hypothesised pathways to inform future data modelling within pain research. The variables and pathways of interest identified as part of this process cover a wide range of concepts considered relevant to the development and maintenance of pain. This included individual factors such as anxiety and loss of identity, interpersonal factors such as disruption to relationships, and the broader role of social worlds. Importantly, the DAG mapped the order of influences and highlighted disruption to relationships as a potential mediating indirect pathway between pain-related experiences and ongoing pain impact. The process also supported translation of experiential, clinical and methodological knowledge into testable research questions for use within existing life-course datasets.
Conclusion: Collaboration using metaphor-based causal diagram development can support multidisciplinary pain research teams to integrate expertise from multiple viewpoints which is vital to ensure that research questions are meaningful to those with chronic pain. The resulting Dream-DAG provides a transparent, theory-informed and experience-informed framework for future empirical analyses, with operationalised and testable hypothesised pathways, although further work is needed to evaluate its transferability to other research teams, datasets and health contexts.

articles.title: Appreciating Ambiguity in Art: The effects of semantic distance and insight confidence on aesthetic appreciation
articles.authors: Rajat Ravi Rao; manon mulckhuyse; Michiel van Elk; Francesco Walker
articles.abstract: Previous work suggests that people tend to more strongly appreciate artworks that they subjectively perceive as more ambiguous. Yet, ambiguity of an artwork has remained difficult to quantify in a standardised and objective way. We introduce a computational, description-based measure to quantify the ambiguity of an artwork, operationalised as the divergence between viewers’ descriptions (semantic distance), alongside a metacognitive measure of insight confidence capturing how confident viewers are in their interpretations. In an online study (N = 123), participants viewed artworks for 6 seconds and either described them and rated their insight confidence, or they provided their subjective aesthetic appreciation by reporting their interest, emotional intensity, and cognitive affect.  Across artworks, greater semantic distance, which indicated higher ambiguity was associated with lower insight confidence. Contrary to preregistered predictions, higher ambiguity was also associated with lower aesthetic appreciation. In contrast, insight confidence showed positive associations with all three appreciation measures. These results show that within our online study aesthetic appreciation is related to how certain a viewer is about what they are viewing rather than the degree of ambiguity of an artwork. Methodologically, this approach provides a generalisable framework for quantifying ambiguity in open-ended responses and dissociating stimulus-driven ambiguity from observers’ metacognitive certainty.

articles.title: Resilience across pandemic phases: distinguishing psychosocial correlates from stress-buffering effects in youth
articles.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Imme Rahmon; Elske Marra; Tinca JC Polderman; Meike Bartels
articles.abstract:
Adolescence and young adulthood are sensitive developmental periods in which stress exposure increases. Youth differ in their capacity to maintain or regain mental health after stressful experiences, reflecting individual differences in resilience. Resilience resources can support mental health by promoting resilient functioning and/or by buffering the association between stress exposure and mental health. The COVID-19 pandemic provides a unique context to investigate these processes across changing stress exposures.
	We examined youth resilience before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic in large Dutch population-based samples, including youth aged 12-25 years before (N = 12,937, 58% female), during (N = 8,934, 58% female), and after the pandemic (N = 37,797, 62% female). We investigated whether loneliness, optimism, and self-rated health were associated with resilient functioning and, to test stress-buffering effects, whether they moderated associations between stress exposure and mental health. Resilient functioning was operationalised as better-than-expected mental health given stress exposure, based on wellbeing, depressive symptoms, and a combination. 
	Higher optimism, lower loneliness, and better self-rated health were consistently associated with higher resilient functioning across pandemic phases and operationalisations (p<.001). Moderation analyses showed inconsistent evidence that these characteristics buffered associations between stress exposure and mental health. 
	Psychosocial characteristics may help explain which youth function better in the context of stress, but do not consistently indicate who is less affected by stress. The results support a view of resilience as a complex and context-dependent process, rather than the result of single protective factors with similar effects across time and contexts.

articles.title: Context Matters, Doesn’t It? The Role of Context in Everyday Emotion Regulation Strategy Use
articles.authors: Anh Tran; Rachel Freeman-Robinson; Peter Koval; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: A common maxim holds that “context is everything”. This perspective transformed the field of emotion-regulation, which evolved from understanding which regulation strategies people use, to understanding how strategy use varies by context (i.e., strategy-situation fit). Theoretical accounts suggest contextual features are crucial in guiding people’s selection of emotion-regulation strategies. However, empirical evidence is isolated in piecemeal studies with inconclusive results. To comprehensively explore context-dependent emotion-regulation, we need data on emotion-regulation across many contexts, at scale. Combining 11 experience-sampling datasets in an integrative analysis (NID=1,720, Nobservations=134,470), we examined how regulation strategy use varies as a function of three theory-derived contextual features—intensity, controllability, and social features (i.e., the presence and closeness of others). We found limited support that context matters for daily emotion-regulation strategy use. Our study provides a well-powered foundational step to test a theory central to emotion-regulation research, and highlights the complexity of capturing strategy-situation fit in daily life.

articles.title: Can a yoga psychology intervention change primal world beliefs?
articles.authors: Sulakshana Kashyap; Jyotsna Agrawal; Shivarama Varambally
articles.abstract: Worldviews play a central role in psychological well-being, yet little research has examined whether fundamental world beliefs (“primals”) can shift following psychological intervention. The present exploratory study examined whether a yoga psychology based 12-session long intervention was associated with changes in primal world beliefs and well-being amongst adults diagnosed with mild-to-moderate depressive disorder (N = 31). Using a single-group pre–post design, participants completed measures of well-being, depressive symptoms, primal world beliefs and Triguna. Results indicated significant improvements in well-being across multiple measures (all p < .001), accompanied by increases in positive primal beliefs (Safe, Enticing, Alive, and Good) and changes in Triguna (increased sattva alongside reductions in rajas and tamas). Informant ratings of triguna traits paralleled self-reports, suggesting observable change. Depressive symptoms also decreased significantly. Findings provide preliminary evidence that shifts in fundamental beliefs toward the world may occur, along with an increase in well-being.

articles.title: The Body Problem: Cautionary Notes on the Embodied Self
articles.authors: Leyla Loued-Khenissi
articles.abstract: Recent years have seen a decisive turn in neuroscience toward embodiment, shifting focus from a brain-bound view of the mind to a more holistic one where the body is treated as constitutive of self and consciousness. While this turn has yielded valuable insights through studies on interoception, multisensory integration and bodily ownership, it also carries significant theoretical and ethical risks. This essay identifies the body problem: the risk of collapsing selfhood into bodyhood, with troubling consequences when applied to bodies that are marginalized or that otherwise do not meet the status quo. Tracing historical debates on mind–body relations, clarifying contemporary notions of the self and examining empirical findings on embodiment, it is argued that strong formulations of the embodied self risk reviving old reductions whereby “less body” implies “less self.” Such reductions threaten to undermine the value of persons whose bodies diverge from normative assumptions. Rather than rejecting embodiment research, this essay calls for caution against its uncritical extension, underscoring the need to guard against theoretical slippage that may entail harmful social consequences.

articles.title: Assessing the added value of process measures for studying gamified learning
articles.authors: Stefan E. Huber; Hanna Rajh-Weber; Rodolpho Luiz Araújo Cortez; Muhterem Dindar; Kristian Kiili; Manuel Ninaus
articles.abstract:
Background: Research on gamified learning typically focuses on assessing learning outcomes. The cognitive-affective processes occurring during learning, and their contributions to learning outcomes, remain comparatively understudied. However, illuminating these processes is essential for optimising digital gamified learning interventions.
Objective: This experimental study evaluates the added value of incorporating process alongside conventional outcome measures, to better understand how gamification may affect learning.
Methods: A total of 121 participants were randomly assigned to a gamified or a non-gamified version of an otherwise equivalent associative learning task. Biometric process measures (heart rate, electrodermal activity, gaze behaviour) were recorded throughout the task. Situated interest and self-efficacy were assessed repeatedly via self-report, alongside post-task cognitive and motivational outcomes. Differences between conditions were quantitatively analysed for both process and outcome measures.
Results and Conclusions: In this laboratory setting, motivational processes and outcomes were surprisingly similar across conditions. In contrast, cognitive process measures revealed a slower learning progress with gamified than non-gamified learning. This was reflected also in biometric process features revealing the extraneous processing demands induced by game design elements. Most importantly, the informativeness of specific biometric features varied by task stage, indicating stage-dependent relevance of different cognitive demands (e.g., encoding, recalling, sustained attention). These findings suggest that gamification’s influence on learning processes is contingent on the task’s cognitive and perceptual affordances and their temporal distribution, a consideration central for the design of individualised, real-time adaptive digital learning systems.

articles.title: Ecological momentary intervention fidelity: Qualitative findings from a habit degradation trial
articles.authors: Robert Edgren; Anine Hess; Jennifer Inauen
articles.abstract: Objectives. Intervention fidelity is critical for interpreting trial outcomes, yet fidelity in digital behaviour change interventions (DBCI) such as ecological momentary interventions (EMIs) is poorly understood. This qualitative study explored participant experiences of intervention fidelity (delivery, receipt, enactment) of a randomised controlled trial (RCT) testing habit degradation strategies including implementation intentions, and the effect of reward on degrading unhealthy snacking habits in daily life. This study aimed to deepen the understanding of intervention fidelity from participants’ perspectives, while also generating generalisable lessons for DBCI. Design. Preregistered semi-structured follow-up interviews. Methods. Twenty-two former RCT participants were purposively sampled for heterogeneity across intervention groups. Interviews were conducted online using personalised graphical elicitation materials. Data were analysed using template analysis, with initial coding informed by three fidelity domains: delivery, receipt, and enactment. Results. Eight themes were identified across three interacting fidelity domains. Delivery concerns included technical disruptions and cue selection that shaped reward delivery. Receipt challenges included mismatches between if-then plans and assigned strategies. Enactment themes revealed that participants generalised behaviour change beyond their if-then plan, pragmatically employed multiple strategies, and were influenced by physical, social, and internal factors. Reactions to reward features were mixed, self-monitoring through the app facilitated behaviour change, and some participants experienced snacking to shift to other situations. Conclusions. This qualitative fidelity study revealed participant-experienced processes—including pragmatic adaptation and self-monitoring reactivity—that typical quantitative fidelity metrics do not capture. These processes should be anticipated in EMI study design, and qualitative fidelity assessment routinely integrated into such research.

articles.title: Forensic Outpatient Cognitive Understanding Study (FOCUS): A study protocol
articles.authors: Juliette Hutten; Hilde Geurts; Tim Ziermans; joan van horn
articles.abstract:
Background: There is growing evidence that cognitive dysfunction plays a role in the emergence and persistence of antisocial behavior, and it is increasingly implicated as relevant for risk assessment and treatment within the Risk-Need-Responsivity (RNR) framework. However, this evidence comes predominantly from prison and inpatient populations. Whether similar patterns hold in forensic outpatient settings remains largely unknown. Moreover, existing studies often rely on normative groups that are not matched for age, sex, and education, and tend to focus on single cognitive domains rather than administering comprehensive test batteries.
Methods: This protocol paper describes the design and methods of the FOCUS study, which aims to map cognitive functioning in forensic outpatients and examine its associations with aggression and treatment outcomes. The study compares forensic outpatients (n = 100) to a normative group (n = 100, matched on sex, age, and educational level). All participants complete a comprehensive computerized neuropsychological test battery covering seven cognitive domains: intelligence, attention, language, executive functioning, social cognition, memory, and decision making. Aggression is assessed using both a self-report questionnaire (Reactive Proactive Questionnaire; RPQ) and a behavioral task (Competitive Reaction Time Task; CRTT). We have four research aims: (1) to compare the cognitive profile of forensic outpatients to a matched normative group; (2) to examine the correspondence between self-reported and task-based aggression; (3) to examine associations between neuropsychological test scores and aggression; and (4) to examine associations between neuropsychological test scores and treatment outcomes, including recidivism risk, treatment non-attendance, dropout, and actual recidivism. 
Discussion: The FOCUS study is the first to administer a comprehensive neuropsychological test battery in a forensic outpatient sample with a matched normative comparison group. Findings are expected to advance understanding of cognitive functioning within the RNR framework and to inform more individualized forensic treatment planning.

articles.title: Auditory Time-to-Contact in the Wild.
articles.authors: William Vallet; Guillaume Lemaitre; Virginie van Wassenhove
articles.abstract: Understanding how the brain processes sensory information to guide goal-directed behavior has been predominantly investigated in controlled laboratory settings. However, ecological environments are characterized by noise, multi-causality, and probabilistic relationships between multisensory sources that may substantially modulate observed behavioral performance. In the present study, we implemented an auditory Time-to-Contact (TTC) task in a wild setting using an in-situ design aboard a French high-speed train (TGV), while participants were exposed to parametrically controlled ecological motion (Forward vs. Backward). Specifically, this setup was intended to manipulate the precision of available sensory information (Poor vs. Reliable) to investigate the flexible reweighting of sensory sources as a function of signal reliability. To understand what drives behavioral performance, we used Bayesian modeling to analyze the accuracy and precision of TTC estimates. This approach dissociates the respective contributions of internal references, sensory precision, and the ecological context. The results demonstrate that the reweighting of sensory sources is not simply driven by task-relevant signal precision but is differentially mediated by the specific conditions of the environment. Mainly, rather than a uniform environmental effect, we observed that ecological consistency situation (Forward motion) overrides task-goal requirements and suppresses the integration of incoming sensory evidence, leading to a systematic behavioral bias. Conversely, the unecological situation (Backward motion) results in behavioral decoupling from the environment, with performance returning to laboratory levels. Together, these findings suggest that internal model inference is highly context-dependent, where ecologically congruent environments can hierarchically dominate task accuracy.

articles.title: Breaking the Cycle: Rewiring Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Through Physical Exercise
articles.authors: Bénédicte Thonon; Damien Brevers
articles.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia commonly exhibit debilitating negative symptoms, including avolition and anhedonia, which represent a significant barrier to engagement in goal-directed behaviours, including physical exercise. They are less physically active than the general population, yet physical exercise is known to improve their symptoms. This narrative review investigates the bidirectional relationship between negative symptoms and physical activity. We propose that negative symptoms hinder engagement in physical activity by altering the cost-benefit analysis of exercise. This is exacerbated by deficits in anticipatory pleasure and reward learning, underpinned by dysfunctions within dopaminergic and glutamatergic circuitry which are critical for motivated behavior. We hypothesise that physical exercise can rewire these deficits through enhanced dopamine transmission, modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic systems, and reduced inflammation. Furthermore, grounded in learning theories and adopting a cognitive-behavioural perspective, this review establishes a theoretical foundation for developing targeted interventions designed to enhance physical activity engagement in this population. We highlight that it is critical to ensure that physical activity is experienced as less effortful and more pleasurable than expected. By generating positive prediction errors (when the experience of exercise is less effortful or more pleasurable than anticipated) exercise helps individuals re-associate it with positive outcomes. Cognitive changes coupled with the biological effects of physical exercise on reward neural pathways are likely to have a synergistic effect, promoting a virtuous cycle of sustained engagement and symptom improvement.

articles.title: Visual Perception in Elite, Fast-Paced Ball-Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Jake Gerard Tiernan; Sarah Lilly Fitzpatrick; Mika Manninen; Catherine Fassbender; Redmond O'Connell; David McGovern
articles.abstract:
Sensory perception – the process through which information from the environment is obtained through the senses and interpreted into meaningful representations – may play a key role in elite sports performance. However, the role of domain-general sensory-perceptual functions in elite sport remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to examine the literature on the sensory perception of elite fast-paced ball sport athletes. Specifically, it aimed to determine whether these athletes possess enhanced sensory perception compared to both sub-elite athletes and non-athletes and whether sensory perception is associated with sport performance metrics.
A systematic literature search of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, including only studies that examined low-level sensory-perceptual functions (e.g.  visual acuity and depth perception) via domain-general tasks. The review focused on elite athletes, as defined by the Participant Classification Framework (McKay et al., 2022).  Three-level meta-analyses with robust variance estimation were conducted on studies comparing elite athletes to both sub-elite athletes and non-athletes. Studies investigating associations between sensory perception and sport performance were described via narrative synthesis.
Twenty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. Eighteen studies compared the visual perception of elite athletes with sub-elite and/or non-athletes, five studies examined the relationship between visual perception and sports performance, while two studies did both. Of the 18 comparative studies, seven studies with non-athlete control groups and six studies with sub-elite control groups met the criteria for meta-analysis; the remaining studies were analysed via narrative synthesis. A large enhancement in visual perception was observed in elite athletes relative to non-athletes (Hedges’ g =1.02, 95% CI: 0.61-1.43, p < 0.01), equating to a 76% probability that a randomly selected elite athlete would outperform a randomly selected non-athlete. No corresponding enhancement was observed in the comparison between elite and sub-elite athletes (Hedges’ g = 0.09, 95% CI: -0.12-0.30, p = 0.33). Furthermore, there was evidence to suggest that enhanced visual perception is associated with better sports performance, particularly for interceptive sports such as baseball and cricket.
The findings from this review highlight that low-level visual perception can differentiate elite athletes from non-athletes, but not athletes from lower competitive levels. These findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of how perceptual processing is shaped by experience, as well as practical implications for the design of vision training protocols aimed at improving sports performance.

articles.title: Lexize-SWE: A quick online test to assess print vocabulary knowledge in Swedish
articles.authors: Rosa Salmela; Raymond Bertram; Lars Bokander; Anna Ingves; Timi Niemensivu; Stefano Garusi; Minna Lehtonen
articles.abstract:
Vocabulary knowledge correlates strongly with general language skills, which is why vocabulary tests
have been used as a proxy for language proficiency. Recently, tests in several languages have been
developed to quickly and reliably assess vocabulary knowledge by means of the visual lexical decision
task. However, such a test does not currently exist for Swedish, a language that is not only spoken in
Sweden, but also by a large minority group in Finland. Lexize-SWE was designed to address this gap.
Lexize-SWE is a 10-minute online test that consists of 52 words and 26 pseudowords. Item performance
was tested with L1 and L2 speakers from both Sweden and Finland (N = 441), followed by a validation
with a new sample (N = 342). The results indicate that the test distinguishes between L1 and L2 speakers.
In L1 speakers, the scores were predicted by age and self-ratings in Swedish. L1 variety (Sweden
Swedish vs. Finland Swedish) was not associated with the test scores. In L2 speakers, the test scores
were predicted by self-ratings, exposure, daily usage of Swedish, language status (L2 speakers with and
without immigrant background), and educational level. In addition, Lexize-SWE scores showed a
moderate correlation with an external Swedish vocabulary test (SweLT). However, the background
factors predicted Lexize-SWE scores more strongly than SweLT scores. Overall, Lexize-SWE appears
suitable for assessing print vocabulary knowledge, particularly in L2 speakers, and is applicable across
both Sweden and Finland contexts. The test is available for free use at https://lexize.org/.

articles.title: From Design to Classroom: How VRT's EDUboxes Tackle Digital Media Literacy for Flemish Young People
articles.authors: Jana Vereecke; Laura Vandenbosch; Kathleen Beullens; Steven Eggermont; Lara Schreurs
articles.abstract: The role of digital media in adolescents' lives is characterized by both opportunities and risks, raising the question of how young people can maximize benefits while minimizing harm. This challenge lies at the heart of digital media literacy (DML), commonly understood as comprising knowledge, attitudes, and skills related to the critical, responsible, and informed use of digital media. Despite assumptions that adolescents naturally acquire these competencies as “digital natives,” research shows substantial inequalities in DML, highlighting the need for structured support. Schools are widely recognized as key environments for fostering DML, yet they often struggle to implement it in a consistent and sustainable way. In Flanders (Belgium), DML is embedded across curricula rather than taught as a separate subject, resulting in fragmented responsibility and limited accountability. To support teachers, tools such as VRT’s EDUboxes have been developed. This chapter focuses on three EDUboxes addressing social media, artificial intelligence (AI), and sexting, each representing distinct but highly relevant domains of adolescents’ digital experiences. These topics illustrate how DML requires an understanding of platform logics, critical evaluation of emerging technologies such as generative AI, and the ability to navigate complex social and ethical situations online. This chapter examines how these EDUboxes are designed to foster DML by analyzing their underlying educational logic. Using a Theory of Change (ToC) approach combined with in-depth interviews with developers, we explore the assumptions, intended outcomes, and pedagogical strategies embedded in these tools, and assess how they align with insights from scientific and grey literature.

articles.title: Successful coordination emerges from aligned self-predictions in a dynamic motor interaction
articles.authors: Prasetia Putra; Fumihiro Kano
articles.abstract: A central challenge in understanding joint action is explaining how individuals achieve successful coordination in dynamic, real-world settings. Although coordination is thought to depend on anticipating future events, including the actions of others, the precise contribution of such predictive processing remains unclear, since most existing evidence comes from simplified laboratory tasks that infer anticipation indirectly from reaction times. To address this gap, we studied 70 participants (forming 64 pairs) during solo and joint sessions of a turn-taking ball-hitting task while recording multimodal behavioral, physiological, demographic, and social measures. We found that successful coordination was most strongly associated with anticipation of one's own action outcomes, outperforming physiological synchrony, motor behavior, demographic characteristics, and social closeness. Partners whose predictions of their own action outcomes were more closely aligned coordinated better, likely because each behaved in ways the other implicitly expected. A Bayesian generative model further showed that well-coordinated pairs relied more heavily on prior expectations than on incoming sensory evidence when generating predictions during joint action. These results suggest that efficient coordination in dynamic real-world tasks emerges primarily when individuals' internal models for predicting their own actions are well aligned across partners. Our quantitative multimodal approach provides a framework for disentangling the contributions of predictive, physiological, motor, and social factors to coordination in naturalistic interactions.

articles.title: Development of the Japanese version of online computerized adaptive tests of young children’s vocabulary: Japanese CDI-CAT
articles.authors: Hiromichi Hagihara; George Kachergis; Virginia A. Marchman; Michael C. Frank; Sho Tsuji
articles.abstract: Measuring children’s early vocabulary is crucial for developmental science and practical applications. The MacArthur–Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDIs) are the most widely used caregiver-report checklist to assess children’s vocabulary across languages and dialects. Although full-length CDIs enable detailed analyses, completing checklists of several hundred words requires considerable time and effort from caregivers, often unnecessarily. Here, building on recent psychometric advances utilizing item response theory (IRT) in languages such as English and Spanish, we developed a computerized adaptive test of the Japanese CDI (Japanese CDI-CAT), which estimates total productive vocabulary size of the full-length CDIs from a reduced number of word items. Using a publicly available Japanese CDI dataset (N = 978) from children aged 12 to 38 months, we compared several IRT models and conducted simulations while varying the number of items administered (25–400). The results showed that the two-parameter logistic IRT model provided the best fit among the candidates. We also found that the CDI-CAT can successfully estimate children’s total vocabulary size while substantially reducing the number of items (e.g., r = .95 with the full-length CDI using only 25–50 items). By extending the CDI-CAT methodology to Japanese, we aim to improve the efficiency of vocabulary assessment and contribute to a more inclusive understanding of early language development across diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

articles.title: On cross-modal commutativity in magnitude production for loudness and brightness
articles.authors: Dorina Kohler; Jürgen Heller
articles.abstract: Can the loudness of a tone be compared to the brightness of a light? The answer is affirmative. We appear to be intuitively capable of making such cross-modal comparisons. Psychophysical research has long assumed that these comparisons are mediated by a common scale of subjective intensity shared across modalities. R.D. Luce (2002, Psychological Review, 109, 520-523) developed a psychophysical theory of magnitude estimation and production based on this assumption and derived empirically testable conditions. In particular, he identified cross-modal commutativity as a key property for empirically evaluating the theory. In an extended, high-powered replication of an experiment reported by W. Ellermeier, F. Kattner, and A. Raum (2021, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 83, 2955-2967), the present study examined this property using a cross-modal magnitude production task for loudness and brightness. Relative to the previous study, individual-level analyses yielded more substantial evidence both for and against crossmodal commutativity, while group-level results remained inconclusive. These findings are discussed in light of a generalized theory that predicts a near-miss to cross-modal commutativity while preserving the assumption of a shared representation of subjective intensity.

articles.title: Let there be information: rethinking cultural evolution
articles.authors: Héctor Marín Manrique; Karl Friston; Michael John WALKER
articles.abstract: Prevailing accounts of cognitive evolution and cumulative culture frequently rely on narrative reconstructions and analogical projections, extrapolating from contemporary human cognition to infer the mental capacities of extinct humans. While such approaches may illuminate recent cultural developments, their applicability to deep prehistory is limited. We propose an alternative framework grounded in the thermodynamic imperative shared by several past and present members of the genus Homo: the reduction of entropy in organism–environment interactions. Central to this framework is the concept of Zones of Bounded Surprisal (ZBS), which formalises adaptive cognition in terms of the capacity to register, tolerate, and integrate new (surprising) information. Rather than treating cultural accumulation as having been continuous, uninterrupted and progressive, ZBS foregrounds information as a driver of evolutionary dynamics relevant in natural selection. We argue that stone-age vagaries of cultural evolution in Homo should be considered from the standpoint of the transmissibility of information between preliterate human beings — with variably evolving ZBS — under different demographic, social, and material constraints. This account foregrounds the role of ZBS in adaptive engagement with novelty and epistemic affordances by extant and extinct Homo.

articles.title: Unpacking the Dual-Path Trust Mechanism Driving Students’ Continuance Intention Toward Campus GenAI: A Hybrid SEM–Machine Learning Approach within the S-O-R Framework
articles.authors: Bingyao Li; Tianzuo Yu
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence agents become embedded in higher education, understanding students' continuance intention (CUI) is critical. To address the underexplored mechanisms regarding how campus AI environments are associated with user trust, this study adopts the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework to investigate a dual-path trust mechanism: AI System-like Trust (AST) and AI Human-like Trust (AHT). Through a hybrid methodology combining Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and non-parametric Random Forest classification, this study analyzes university students' CUI toward campus GenAI. The findings demonstrate that Information Quality (IQ) and Service Quality (SQ) are positively associated with both AST and AHT pathways. Conversely, Facilitating Conditions (FC) and Performance Expectancy (PE) do not exhibit independent linear associations within the simultaneous structural estimation. Rather than indicating an empirical absence of functional value, this configuration uncovers a holistic evaluation mechanism among digital natives, where basic functional affordances operate as baseline hygiene constraints whose variance is subsumed by quality attributes. Notably, while both AST and AHT exert concurrently significant linear driving forces on CUI within the structural path framework, the exploratory machine learning analysis clarifies that under recursive partitioning, AHT exhibits a higher relative predictive weight. Furthermore, a localized asymmetry operates within the linear mediation channels, where SQ selectively mobilizes AHT over AST to drive continuous usage. Post-hoc inspections imply that PE operates through a non-linear threshold dynamic, transitioning into an active predictive catalyst primarily within the positive spectrum of user perception. Our study contributes to campus AI services evaluation by highlighting that within the contemporary GenAI ecosystem, students' evaluative focus prioritizes relational and epistemic quality over functional accessibility. Campus application administrators and developers are advised to prioritize content rigor and responsive, empathetic interaction design to cultivate the relational trust relevant for sustained engagement.

articles.title: Is GenAI Helpful for Writing? A Re-Analysis Using Robust Meta-Analysis (RoBMA)
articles.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis showed that genAI has a strong impact on writing. The current analysis instead shows that the effects are negligible after correcting for heterogeneity and publication bias.

articles.title: Using Classification Trees to Identify the Best Method in Monte Carlo Simulations: From Population Parameters to Observed Features
articles.authors: Jeongwon Choi; Hao Wu
articles.abstract: Monte Carlo simulations are widely used to compare statistical methods, but their findings are often difficult to interpret and rarely translate into practical guidelines. This gap arises for two reasons. First, method performance often depends on complex interactions among simulation factors that conventional summaries fail to detect. Second, performance is typically evaluated against population values that are unknown in practice, whereas applied researchers see only features of their sample data. We build on the classification tree approach to address both problems, adding two pruning strategies for the simulation context: a combined procedure that accounts for equivalent representations of the same data, and effect-size-based pruning that prevents large numbers of replications from inflating tree complexity. We illustrate it with zero cell correction strategies for estimating tetrachoric correlations. In Example 1, we reanalyze results from Choi and Wu (2026) using the original simulation factors as predictors, yielding clear decision rules that still rely on population values. In Example 2, we generate data under continuous simulation factors and construct predictors directly from observed 2X2 contingency tables, so the rules can be applied to real data. More broadly, the framework provides an approach for translating Monte Carlo comparisons of competing methods into practical guidelines.

articles.title: Trait Apathy and Fatigue are Associated with Diminished Academic Functioning Among University Students Aged 30 - 50
articles.authors: Mindaugas Jurgelis; Monica Copko; Christopher Leaver; Lachlan White; Josiah Cameron Krieg
articles.abstract: Motivation is critical to successful academic functioning. A growing body of evidence details how motivation evolves throughout the lifetime, yet middle adulthood is rarely examined. Here we examined how trait apathy and fatigue, both of which manifest in diminished motivation, relate to self-reported academic functioning among university students aged 30 – 50. 332 students completed trait apathy and fatigue scales, measures of academic functioning (autonomous motivation, controlled motivation, study engagement, study effort, academic stress, dropout intentions, academic performance, and study satisfaction), and measures of family, household, work-related factors. Apathy and fatigue were related to almost all academic measures, yet apathy was more closely linked to academic functioning; in particular autonomous motivation, study engagement, and study satisfaction. Our results suggest that relatively stable individual differences in motivation among healthy adults, as captured by the measures of trait-apathy and fatigue, are closely linked to functioning in a critical area – academic development.

articles.title: Syllables, not words, minutes, or utterances, to accurately characterize verbal input to children
articles.authors: Meg Cychosz
articles.abstract: The verbal input that children hear from caregivers around them can explain some of the well-known variability in trajectories of early child language development. Verbal input has traditionally been quantified by counting words, minutes, or utterances of child-directed speech from an adult interlocutor. This paper argues that exclusive reliance on these units can result in inaccurate estimation of verbal input, especially when comparisons are made between different languages, sociocultural settings, and speakers. Using spontaneous speech data from children and adults, we illustrate some confounds that these units create. Though illustrated with children’s verbal input, these confounds apply to any quantification of language structure across speakers, registers, or languages. We show that words, which vary in internal grammatical complexity between and even within speakers and individual languages, result in cross-linguistic and speaker age confounds. Utterances are likewise confounded with typological differences and speaker age. Minutes, which appear to be language-neutral, are in fact confounded with speaking rate which similarly varies within and between speakers, languages, and registers, especially since children speak slower than adults. We put forth measures based instead in information theory that employ the syllable as the base unit to resolve many of these issues: total information transmitted (syllable count x information density per syllable) and information rate (information density x syllable rate). These results demonstrate that accurate characterization of children’s verbal input requires paying close attention to linguistic structure and speaker attributes, and that information-theoretic measures can provide more reliable estimates across languages, speakers, and registers.

articles.title: On Why Meta-d′ May Not Go the Distance: Confidence Distance as a Calibration-Based Measure of Metacognition
articles.authors: Domenic Groh
articles.abstract: Meta-d' is widely used to quantify metacognitive sensitivity, and the meta-d'/d' ratio, commonly referred to as the M-ratio, is interpreted as metacognitive efficiency. However, both depend on assumptions inherited from signal detection theory, including Gaussian evidence distributions and a shared latent evidence axis for type-1 decisions and confidence judgments. These assumptions are not guaranteed in many behavioral paradigms. The present paper examines how violations of these assumptions affect meta-d' and the M-ratio, and introduces Confidence Distance as a calibration-based measure of metacognitive performance. Confidence Distance is defined as the mean absolute distance between trial-wise confidence and objective correctness after mapping confidence ratings onto the unit interval. Across simulation studies, non-Gaussian evidence distributions distorted the M-ratio even when metacognitive monitoring was ideal. These distortions were not limited to underestimation: heavy-tailed and light-tailed evidence inflated the ratio, whereas skewed evidence reduced it. In addition, when confidence was based on evidence not used for the type-1 response, meta-d' itself became inflated despite unchanged metacognitive ability. Confidence Distance, by contrast, remained comparatively stable across distributional forms, increased monotonically when metacognitive noise was added, and remained well-defined across multidimensional and multi-alternative task structures because it requires only trial-wise correctness and confidence. These findings suggest that meta-d' and the M-ratio conflate metacognitive performance with distributional misspecification or evidence-axis mismatch in applied research contexts. Confidence Distance therefore offers a transparent and assumption-light index of confidence–accuracy correspondence.

articles.title: "It's a balancing act": Autistic fathers navigating parenting in everyday life
articles.authors: Chris Edwards; Abigail Love; Ru Ying Cai; Kees-jan Archbald; Dean Dickson; Sean Hynes; Abel Trindade; Sarah Edwards; Bronwyn Leigh; Vicki Gibbs
articles.abstract:
Background
Autistic parents are increasingly recognized as an important source of insight into Autistic adulthood and family life, yet the perspectives of Autistic people who identify as fathers remain almost entirely absent from research. Fathers have distinct experiences, and the absence of their stories and perspectives limits understanding of Autistic parenting more broadly. This study addressed this gap by exploring how Autistic fathers understand and experience parenting across the lifespan.
Methods
We co-produced the study with four Autistic fathers who contributed to design, interview development, and analysis. Nineteen Autistic fathers took part in semi-structured interviews, either spoken or written, depending on their preference. We analyzed the data using reflexive thematic analysis informed by constructionist and participatory research principles.
Results
Our analysis generated five themes: (1) Finding joy and meaning in everyday moments, which captured the emotional rewards of fatherhood; (2) Becoming myself through fatherhood, describing how parenting strengthened self-understanding and Autistic identity; (3) Walking the tightrope of family life, reflecting the effort of balancing sensory, emotional, and practical demands; (4) Parenting as relational work, showing how fathers negotiated understanding and communication within family relationships and the tension that arose when they felt misunderstood; and (5) Parenting in systems stacked against us, highlighting the barriers encountered in services and wider society.
Conclusion
Autistic fathers’ accounts deepen understanding of Autistic adulthood and family life. Their experiences show that fatherhood can strengthen identity and connection while exposing the limits of systems that rarely recognize Autistic needs. These fathers’ insights call for change in how research, policy, and services engage with Autistic people and their families.

articles.title: Daily fluctuations in delay discounting and smartphone-based multimodal measures track nighttime drinking in alcohol use disorder: A 28-day monitoring study
articles.authors: Hyeonmin Lee; Manjae Kwon; Jeung-Hyun Lee; Mina Kwon; Suyeon Song; Deokjong Lee; Jung-Seok Choi; Young-Chul Jung; Woo-Young Ahn
articles.abstract:
Background and Aims:
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves day-to-day fluctuations in cognitive, psychological, and contextual factors that are difficult to fully capture using retrospective or cross-sectional assessment alone. Computational markers, such as discounting rate, ambiguity tolerance, and risk preference, may provide useful indicators of day-level drinking risk, but have rarely been assessed repeatedly in real-world settings or examined together with daily app-based self-reports and passive smartphone-derived measures. This study examined whether these multimodal day-level measures were associated with same-day nighttime drinking, focusing on whether within-person changes in computational markers remained associated with drinking after accounting for concurrent self-reported and contextual measures.

Design:
A 28-day longitudinal observational study using repeated smartphone-based assessments and passive sensing.

Setting:
Daily-life smartphone-based monitoring of community-recruited participants in the Republic of Korea.

Participants:
The final analytic sample included 143 adults meeting DSM-5 criteria for AUD.

Measurements:
The primary outcome was same-day nighttime drinking, assessed using daily app-based self-reports. Daily predictors covered three domains. App-based self-reports included mood, alcohol craving, meal intake, and sleep-related variables. Computational predictors were derived from delay discounting and choice under risk and ambiguity tasks. Passive smartphone-derived predictors included time spent at home, calls, steps, and foreground app use. Generalized linear mixed-effects models examined associations between nighttime drinking and multimodal predictors decomposed into within-person and between-person components.

Findings:
A multimodal model integrating computational parameters, daily app-based self-reports, and passive smartphone-derived measures showed the highest explanatory power for same-day nighttime drinking (marginal R² = 0.22). In this final model, higher within-person delay discounting [log(k)], alcohol craving, and positive mood, as well as lower meal intake and percent time at home, were associated with a higher likelihood of nighttime drinking. At the between-person level, only lower average meal intake was associated with a higher likelihood of nighttime drinking. Within-person fluctuations in log(k) were largely uncorrelated with other day-level predictors and showed no clear next-day association.

Conclusions:
Associations with same-day nighttime drinking were observed primarily at the within-person level, suggesting that day-level changes may be more informative than stable individual differences. Within-person increases in delay discounting remained associated with nighttime drinking after accounting for other modalities, suggesting that multimodal monitoring may help identify periods of elevated drinking risk.

articles.title: Behavioral and Neural Differences of Cognitive Control in Child Musicians
articles.authors: Jed Villanueva; B. Rael Cahn; Assal Habibi
articles.abstract: Monolingual 8-12-year-old musicians (N = 42, M age = 10.51) and nonmusicians (N = 38, M age = 10.24) completed two executive function tasks: a visual go/no-go task and an auditory oddball task. Analysis of their behavioral and neural data revealed group differences in response efficiency and cognitive control. Behaviorally, musicians responded faster to correct go trials on the go/no-go task without compromising discrimination ability (d’). Exploratory analysis of event-related potentials (ERPs) indexing error monitoring revealed that musicians have a larger error positivity (Pe) amplitude at Pz in response to incorrect responses on no-go trials. Contrary to our preregistered hypothesis, analyses of early auditory evoked potentials demonstrated a more negative N2 amplitude among musicians in response to distractors. This finding may reflect increased recruitment of neural processes involved in conflict monitoring and the discrimination of target from non-target stimuli. Although musicians were generally older and from more economically privileged backgrounds, the observed behavioral and neural differences remained evident in exploratory analyses restricted to age- and socioeconomic status-matched participants These findings provide supporting evidence for an association between music training and cognitive control in middle childhood, contributing to a growing body of literature suggesting that musical engagement may contribute to the development of cognitive control and other behavioral and cognitive capacities during childhood.

articles.title: The Nature of Mind-Wandering to Secrets.
articles.authors: Valentina Bianchi; Katharine Greenaway; Sarah Taylor O'Brien; Janine Griffiths; Kate NW Kim; Ella Moeck; Michael Slepian; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: Secrets are on people’s minds more than they are held back in conversation. Research suggests that such mind-wandering to secrets can be problematic for well-being, yet the mechanisms behind this link are still unclear. To better understand what may underlie the harm of mind-wandering to secrets, we conducted two studies. First, in a 14-day daily diary study (Study 1, N = 240) we investigated what people think about when mind-wandering to their secrets, and how these thoughts come to mind in daily life—spontaneously or deliberately. Worries and concerns about secrets intruded on the mind spontaneously, whereas when people intentionally mind-wandered to a secret, they fantasized and daydreamt about it (Study 1). Second, in a 7-day experience-sampling study (Study 2, N = 207) we probed the directionality of relationships between the two types of mind-wandering and affective experiences about secrets. Across studies, when secrets came to mind spontaneously, but not deliberately, people reported feeling greater negative emotion both in the moment (Study 1 and 2) and approximately 2 hours later (Study 2). This work offers the first investigation into spontaneous and deliberate mind-wandering to the same target content in daily life, capturing the temporal dynamics between mind-wandering and emotional well-being. Our findings point to spontaneous mind-wandering to secrets as a primary player in the well-being costs of secrecy. By yielding insights into the way secrets weigh on people’s minds, this research suggests possible ways to manage the well-being costs of secrets in everyday life.

articles.title: Gender differences in Academic Stress and Academic Pressure among students aged 18-23 in Sri Lanka
articles.authors: Shameeshika Kuhandran
articles.abstract: Nearly 75% of students experience academic stress and pressure across the globe. There can be gender differences in perceiving and managing academic stress. The present study explored to identify the gender differences among the school and college students who experience academic stress and academic pressure. The sample consists of 58 students in total aged 18-23, 39 female students and 19 male students. They were chosen by purposive and snowball sampling method and the data was collected by an online based survey using the Google forms. Students were assessed with; Demographic questionnaires, Academic Stress Scale (ASS) and Academic Pressure Scale (APS). The collected data was analysed using IBM SPSS 25 version. To assess the hypotheses; Pearson correlation, Independent t-tests and ANOVA test were conducted. The findings of the study revealed that almost 45% of the participants in Sri Lanka experience academic stress and there is a strong positive correlation between academic stress and academic pressure. But, there were no gender differences among the sample in academic stress and academic pressure. Also, there were negative significant relationships between other demographic variables and academic stress. The students stated the major academic stressors were high workload, peer pressure and worrying about grades or results. Thus, every student who experience academic stress are prone to psychological disorders, there should be implications developed in order to maintain a stress-free, positive school and college environments.

articles.title: Learning progress shapes people's voluntary engagement
articles.authors: Ionatan Kuperwajs; Wei Ji Ma
articles.abstract: A key aspect of naturalistic behavior is that engagement with a task itself is typically voluntary. Studying the decision to continue engaging with a task or not requires experiments to be constructed such that subjects always have the option to participate over a long time horizon. While this is difficult to achieve in traditional laboratory settings, the introduction of large-scale data sets in cognitive science has enabled the design of studies that are suitable for directly investigating voluntary engagement. In this work, we study how people's learning progress shapes their motivation to play when they are provided with complete autonomy over their own participation. Our data set consists of 1,234,844 people playing a challenging variant of tic-tac-toe. We use continuous measures of performance and the timing of gameplay to operationalize learning and motivation over many months, conducting analyses guided by the literature on skill acquisition and intrinsic motivation. We first establish a correlation between task performance and total experience. Then, we show that people exhibit robust signatures of learning as well as persistent behavior and a preference for intermediate challenges. Finally, we propose a process-level model of human learning that predicts latency between games by formalizing our empirical findings as changes in playing strength with respect to the time that games are played. Overall, our work provides a computational description of human behavior in a real-world environment where choosing to engage at all is a meaningful decision.

articles.title: Coherence Across Tasks In the Development of Counterfactual Reasoning
articles.authors: Michelle Wong; Rosie Aboody; Eva Rafetseder; Jonathan F. Kominsky; Elizabeth Bonawitz
articles.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning -- the ability to consider what could, would, or should have happened alongside what actually occurred -- is foundational to causal understanding, learning from experience, and making sense of others’ minds. While this skill emerges in early childhood, its developmental trajectory remains debated. How does this ability develop and what other constructs is it related to? To investigate, we explored the development of counterfactual reasoning through a 14-item unmoderated online battery measuring counterfactual reasoning across narrative, physical, and causal-machine domains in 320 children (ages 3-7). We found steady improvement on the tasks, with performance improving over early to middle childhood. Performance was also positively correlated within all three tasks, controlling for age and performance on non-counterfactual cognitive tasks, suggesting that all three domains were tapping into a similar underlying counterfactual ability. Additionally, children who responded correctly on narrative counterfactuals that could not be solved using heuristic shortcuts performed better across the other counterfactual tasks (Study 1) and Theory of Mind tasks (Study 2). These findings provide evidence for a latent construct underlying counterfactual reasoning and introduce a validated tool for future research.

articles.title: EEG dynamics during prolonged Samatha meditation:  A case study across levels of meditation expertise
articles.authors: Yuta Naito; Tomohisa Asai; Aya Katayama; Mina Wakabayashi; Hiroshi Imamizu; Kenryo Minowa
articles.abstract: This case study examined differences in the temporal dynamics of EEG indices as a function of meditation expertise using a quantitative analytic framework. EEG was recorded and analyzed across multiple sessions over three days during prolonged Samatha meditation in two meditation novices and two expert meditators. Alpha-band power, beta-band power, and peak alpha frequency were extracted in 1-min bins and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. These models revealed significant expertise × time interactions for beta-band power and peak alpha frequency. Within-group analyses showed that beta-band power decreased over time in the novice group, whereas beta-band power and peak alpha frequency increased over time in the expert group. These findings suggest that EEG indices during prolonged Samatha meditation may exhibit temporal dynamics that differ according to meditation expertise. The results also highlight the utility of analyzing EEG during meditation as a temporally unfolding process rather than only as session-level averages. In addition, a supplementary analysis using an external dataset was conducted to compare the present findings and to examine the applicability of the analytic approach. The supplementary analysis revealed patterns that differed from those observed in the primary dataset. This discrepancy underscores the need to consider factors such as meditation style, practice duration, participant characteristics, and measurement context when interpreting inconsistent findings in meditation EEG research.

articles.title: Voluntary Musical Imagery Use in Musicians’ Mental Practice: Functional Orientations and Pedagogical Implications
articles.authors: Chen Meng; Henna-Riikka Peltola; Geoff Luck
articles.abstract: Mental practice is widely recognized as a useful strategy in musicians’ learning and performance preparation, with voluntary musical imagery (VMI) offering one means through which musicians may rehearse and organize music internally. Yet less is known about how musicians use VMI within routine mental practice. To investigate this, semi-structured interviews with 15 classically trained instrumentalists were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Findings indicate that participants described VMI as an analytical, self-regulated practice strategy. This strategy was organized around two functional orientations: music-task-focused VMI and performance-situation-focused VMI. The former directed imagery toward musical material, while the latter directed imagery toward the broader conditions of performance. VMI use was reported as enhancing performance confidence, musical understanding, and memorization. However, participants also reported adverse experiences, including intrusive imagery or anxiety when it was difficult to verify imagined work physically, as well as constraints on VMI use related to cognitive overload, time pressure, emotional state, and limited pedagogical guidance. Taken together, the study offers a use-oriented understanding of VMI in naturalistic mental practice and suggests that music education may support VMI use through clearer task definition, strategy instruction, and attention to affective regulation.

articles.title: The "i" in team insight predicting performance above and beyond collective competence
articles.authors: Robert Ward; James Hardy; Paul Rauwolf; Gemma Chatten
articles.abstract: Teams often outperform their individual members, yet the mechanisms underlying this advantage remain poorly understood. A dominant account holds that teams benefit from confidence-weighted integration of member judgments — but this relies on confidence being an accurate signal of competence. Here we investigate whether metacognitive insight, the accuracy with which individuals evaluate their own and their team's performance, predicts team accuracy above and beyond member competence and confidence. In a laboratory study, 358 adults completed a matrix reasoning task individually and then in teams of three or four (N = 111 teams), providing retrospective estimates of their own and their team's accuracy. We distinguished two forms of insight: self-insight (calibration between estimated and actual individual accuracy) and team-insight (calibration between estimated and actual team accuracy).
