articles.title: The IP Paradox for New Zealand Scientific Start-Ups: Navigating Value and Impediment in Technology Transfer
articles.authors: Sam Mutsamwira
articles.abstract:
This study examines how scientist-entrepreneurs in New Zealand experience and navigate intellectual property (IP) during the technology transfer process. Using interpretative phenomenological analysis, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with fourteen scientist-entrepreneurs, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal a central IP Paradox; IP is simultaneously an indispensable prerequisite for technology transfer and a significant impediment. Useful theories, the Innovation Incentive Theory, Knowledge Spillover Theory of Entrepreneurship, and Resource-Based View, only partially explain this phenomenon, as managing IP introduces profound strategic tensions, costs, and uncertainties. The analysis elucidates the IP Paradox for scientific start-ups, which complements and adds on to these dominant theoretical frameworks, and then develops an IP Navigation Matrix as a sense-making and decision-support tool grounded in entrepreneurs’ lived experience. This provides a nuanced understanding of IP’s dual role, offering direct managerial and policy implications for improving technology transfer, supporting academic entrepreneurship, and fostering innovation in New Zealand and other small open economies. The findings also provide practical insights for IP practitioners advising scientific ventures in New Zealand.

Keywords: intellectual property protection; scientific start-ups; patents; trade secrets; technology transfer; New Zealand

articles.title: Every Methodology is a Weapon if you Hold it Right: Union-Led Well-Being Measurement as an Act of Collective Resistance
articles.authors: Jon Mendel; Taylor G. Hill
articles.abstract: Workplace well-being surveys are typically led by employers in a hierarchical, top-down way, treating distress as a problem on the individual scale rather than a collective condition. Drawing on Marston et al.’s (2005) critique of hierarchical scale, this paper reimagines well-being measurement by developing a democratic practice of industrial participation and epistemic resistance that offers more horizontal points of entry. As part of a union-led case study at the University of Dundee, Scotland, we examine how a community-driven initiative co-designed and administered a well-being survey during a period of acute institutional crisis (N = 84). Survey findings indicated near-universal burnout with widespread physical and psychological ill-health, reports of excessive unsustainable workloads, low autonomy, and eroded organisational trust. The paper shows that that participatory data practices can represent horizontal infrastructures of care and that these practices work as both evidence of harm and as revolutionary theory in Harvey’s (2009: 152) terms: engaging with status quo ideas like well-being to provide “them with real content, and using them to identify real choices immanent in the present”. We draw on theories of pragmatism to discuss how radicalising well-being measurement extends industrial democracy by shifting the means of knowledge production: workers define and evidence their own realities, transforming surveys from tools of managerial oversight into practices of solidarity and weapons for resistance. To resist the use of well-being measurement as a tool of hierarchical government, we aim to show that every methodology can be a weapon if you use it right.

articles.title: Parental separation in childhood and development of political party identification in young adulthood
articles.authors: Lena Wagner
articles.abstract: Party identification is widely recognised as a pillar of democratic stability and a driver of political participation rooted in family socialisation. Although parental separation has become increasingly common across Europe, little is known about its implications for political socialisation. This study examines how parental separation during childhood (ages 0-15) affects the probability of identifying with any political party across the developmental trajectory of young adulthood (ages 18-25) by estimating logistic mixed-effects growth models on longitudinal mother-child dyadic data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (years 2001-2024; N = 2,770). Growing up with a partisan mother emerges as the strongest predictor of party identification, while maternal education exerts an independent effect and parental separation shows a modest negative association. Effects are largely confined to initial levels at age 18, pointing to early and persistent stratification. Going beyond average effects, results indicate that separation weakens mother-child transmission, particularly following early-childhood separation, while having little impact among offspring of apartisan mothers. Additional analyses suggest that weakened transmission cannot be explained by father absence alone but may reflect complex post-separation family dynamics.

articles.title: What makes or breaks newly-cohabs? Couples’ gender attitudinal pairings and their union trajectories
articles.authors: Daniele Florean; Natalie Nitsche
articles.abstract: While declining marriage and rising cohabitation are not new, less partnering, more breakups, and rising singlehood are novel and poorly understood trends. How newly cohabiting couples' joint gender attitudes predict their relationship trajectories, and whether this varies across social contexts, is hence an important yet underresearched question. Using data from the German Family Panel (pairfam), we follow 1,297 newly formed couples, investigating how their gender attitudinal pairings evolve and predict breakups or marriage transitions, leveraging East-West German gender climate differences to assess contextual moderation. Our findings extend the literature in three ways. First, gender climate context matters for marriage transitions: among West but not East German couples, joint traditionalism is associated with more than twice the marriage transition rate of attitudinally mismatched couples. Second, attitudinal convergence among initially mismatched couples (the majority in our sample) emerges as the strongest predictor of both higher marriage rates and lower breakup risks across both regions. Third, the gender normative context appears to interact with attitudinal pairings in whether couples marry but not in whether they stay together. This suggests intra-couple psychological processes are a key predictor of family formation dynamics and deserve more attention in demographic research.

articles.title: The Measurement Crisis in Cognitive Warfare Defence: Evaluating Single-Layer Countermeasures across Democratic Societies
articles.authors: Cezar Vasilescu
articles.abstract:
State-sponsored cognitive warfare has emerged as a defining cross-national security challenge, systematically targeting the information environments of democratic societies and allied institutions. Yet despite the proliferation of defensive countermeasures since 2020, systematic evidence evaluation remains critically limited. This research examines four major individual intervention categories (prebunking and inoculation theory, artificial intelligence detection technologies, media literacy programmes, and rapid response systems) through structured evidence synthesis applying adapted GRADE criteria.
Two research objectives guide the analysis: evaluating empirical evidence quality and identifying measurement limitations that systematically overestimate operational effectiveness; and analysing performance gaps between laboratory conditions and real-world deployment. Evidence reveals substantial variation in empirical support across countermeasure categories. Prebunking demonstrates the strongest evidence base, with large-scale field studies showing 55-60% improvements in manipulation detection. AI detection systems show 45-50% accuracy degradation from laboratory to operational conditions due to adversarial adaptation.
The research identifies a fundamental measurement problem: over 89% of studies analysed measure capabilities rather than behaviours, creating systematic overestimation of intervention effectiveness. These findings provide evidence-grounded guidance for national security planners, defence ministries, and NATO member states allocating resources to cognitive defence, emphasising behavioural validation as a prerequisite for operational confidence.

articles.title: Communal Activities as Intercultural Communication Strategies of Social Actors in Developing Social Cohesion in Sudiroprajan
articles.authors: Buddy Riyanto; Andrik Purwasito; Andre Noevi Rahmanto; Sri Hastjarjo
articles.abstract: This article examines communal activities as intercultural communication strategies used by local social actors to develop social cohesion in Sudiroprajan, Surakarta, Indonesia. Sudiroprajan is a multicultural urban neighborhood in which Javanese residents, Chinese Indonesians, Javanese-Chinese descendants, and communities with diverse religious, generational, occupational, and socio-economic backgrounds interact in everyday life. Using a qualitative approach within a constructivist paradigm and a grounded theory strategy, this study draws on observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation of community practices. The findings show that Grebeg Sudiro, Barongsai Macan Putih, neighborhood collective work, Kampung Pelangi, the Harapan Kita Waste Bank, the Suka Maju Women Farmers Group, and the Sinar Mentari Climate Village Program operate as communicative arenas where residents encounter difference, negotiate meanings, coordinate roles, reproduce local values, and create shared experiences. Social actors, including community leaders, neighborhood administrators, religious figures, women’s groups, youth, cultural activists, and environmental organizers, act as initiators, mobilizers, facilitators, mediators, and interpreters of meaning. The article argues that communal activities are not merely socio-cultural or environmental programs; they constitute an infrastructure of intercultural communication that transforms diversity into social capital, strengthens trust, and supports inclusive community identity.

articles.title: Enabling Sustainability Transitions in the Semiconductor Domain: Designing a Transition Practice–Education Cycle
articles.authors: Hiromi Kimoto; Maoko Fujisaki; Keito Inoue; Norio Kamitsubo; Sota Takagi; Kohei Saito; Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: Semiconductors are enabling technologies whose innovation is largely governed by technical roadmaps, leaving limited infrastructure for the normative deliberation and capability-building required for sustainability transitions. This paper asks how transition agenda formation can be connected to university-based education and project formation in the semiconductor sector. Drawing on Transition Design and Transition Management, we conceptualize the Transition Practice–Education Cycle (TPEC), a process framework that iteratively links transition agenda formation with industry and domain frontrunners, university-based Transition Design education, and project formation with committed stakeholders. Using Research through Design, we report an initial TPEC implementation at Institute of Science Tokyo in the semiconductor domain. The analysis identifies two translation functions absent from the initial design: Agenda-to-Education Translation and Project Translation and Validation. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a revised TPEC framework that embeds both as explicit design functions. The study also suggests Transition-oriented Semiconductor Capability as a potential educational goal for enabling technology sectors.

articles.title: Beyond the Takeover: Youth Gatherings, Urban Public Space, and the Racialization of Disorder in Chicago
articles.authors: Almethia C. Franklin
articles.abstract:
In recent years, Chicago has witnessed a significant rise in large-scale youth gatherings in high-visibility public spaces. Labeled "teen takeovers" in dominant media and policy discourse, these events are almost exclusively framed as public safety threats requiring law enforcement response. This paper argues that this framing is both analytically insufficient and politically consequential. Drawing on preliminary media and news analysis, an emerging qualitative research agenda, and a multi-disciplinary theoretical framework, this paper reframes youth gatherings as social phenomena that reveal fundamental dynamics of race, space, territorial boundary, and urban belonging. We identify three dimensions that existing scholarship has not yet systematically examined: (1) the role of social media and digital technology in organizing, escalating, and documenting these events; (2) the apparent dissolution of hyperlocal territorial boundaries historically maintained by street organizations in Chicago; and (3) the variation in form, activity, and framing of analogous youth gatherings across U.S. cities. We situate these dimensions within a five-part theoretical architecture drawing on moral panic theory, critical criminology, spatial theory, Black cultural studies, and the sociology of punishment. We conclude by presenting a research agenda for empirical investigation and discussing the implications of this work for policy and community response.

Keywords: youth gatherings, teen takeovers, urban public space, moral panic, territorial boundaries, Chicago, racialization, social media, cultural criminology

articles.title: Algorithmic Decision Making in Medical Diagnosis: Understanding The Ambiguity Present Within Australian Law and 'Explainable Artificial Intelligence'
articles.authors: James Scheibner; Khevalin Parekh
articles.abstract: This paper assesses whether Australian medical device regulation, tort and privacy law impose a requirement for artificial intelligence based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) to be explainable. The paper analyses the concept of ‘explainability’ through a framework developed by Ferretti, Schneider and Blasimme (2018) which divides algorithmic opacity into three categories: lack of disclosure, epistemic opacity and explanatory opacity. These three categories of opacity concern varying levels of understanding of algorithmic outcomes by different audiences. This paper first examines whether medical device regulations in Australia impose a duty on medical device manufacturers to ensure machine learning powered CDSS tools are explainable. This paper then assesses whether Australian negligence law imposes an equivalent obligation on medical practitioners. Finally, this paper examines whether recent Australian privacy law reforms impose a requirement of explainability. This paper concludes that each of the three branches of law imposes a requirement for medical device manufacturers and practitioners to disclose when machine learning is used in CDSS tools. However, there is no further legal obligation to explain how these tools make decisions, or why they reach particular decisions.

articles.title: Internal Dispossession: A Sovereignty-Grounded Theory of the Harms of American Indian Identity Theft
articles.authors: Cynthia Greywolf
articles.abstract:
American Indian identity theft (self-indigenization, pretendianism) is usually treated as one
person’s deception. I argue that it is something larger. This article presents Internal
Dispossession Theory (IDT), a sovereignty-grounded theory of the harms of American Indian
identity theft. Its premise is that identity theft is the latest form of colonial dispossession: as
Native land and resources were taken, so too is the authority of tribal nations to say who belongs,
relocated from the nation onto individuals, institutions, and markets. That relocation produces
relational, structural, and epistemic harms that culminate in internal dispossession: the erosion of
a tribal nation’s capacity to define itself, lived also by the individual Native person whose place a
counterfeit takes. Stated as nine propositions and grounded in a sovereign autoethnography of a
documented case, IDT names a contemporary colonial mechanism. Its remedy is not institutional
gatekeeping but tribal self-determination.

articles.title: Islam, Reason and Modernity in Colonial India: a Comparative Study of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali
articles.authors: NAFIS HAIDER
articles.abstract:
The paper examines the debates around reason and rationality in Islam, particularly in the works of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali, locating their modernist articulation in the backdrop of socio-political context of colonial India. In the aftermath of the revolt of 1857, Muslims in India were subjected to institutional marginalisation, incarceration, civilisational stigma and intensified suspicion. As the orientalist discourse portrayed Muslims and Islam as an irrational, oriental and despotic tradition, it rendered Muslims political claims vulnerable to discrimination under colonial modernity. This crisis of political exclusion pushed for an articulation of Islam as a rational and ethical tradition. 
The paper argues that Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali reinterpreted Islam as a rational tradition which transcends mere theological category and served also as a political strategy of survival, locating Islam and Muslims as legitimate ethical civilisation. Sir Syed grounds his interpretation of Islam in a rationalist hermeneutics, through natural law and scientific reason which aimed at making Islamic tradition intelligible to colonial epistemology, enabling education, political participation and representation. Syed Ameer Ali while running on the similar thread, works along a parallel pathway of juridical and historical reasoning to defend Islam as a moral and constitutional epistemology. Though differing in methodology and approach, both thinkers rearticulated Islam as compatible with the changing world order. Through a comparative study of these two thinkers, the paper tries to identify the different and multiple rationalities within the framework of Islamic modernism in Colonial India.
The paper states that this political idiom of survival and legitimacy works in extending and reshaping Muslim reformist thought, reoriented debate on constitutional politics, representation and institutional arrangement in colonial India. By foregrounding reason as a political strategy, the paper contributes to the intellectual history of Islam in South Asia and the ways through which modernist Islamic discourse negotiated through power, exclusion and belongingness under colonial rule in India.

Keywords: Islam, Muslim, Colonialism, Modernity, Political exclusion, South Asia

articles.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles.authors: Pyung Kim
articles.abstract: This study exploits South Korea’s unique dual-policy, in which an emissions trading scheme (ETS) and a command-and-control program (Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel, to compare carbon pricing with prescriptive regulation at the firm level. Using a difference-in-differences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that ETS-regulated firms reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to TMS firms, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. These reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation, pointing to the importance of incentive-based policy design.

articles.title: Projecting Intergenerational Family Structures  over the Life Course:  Empirical and Simulated Populations in Norway
articles.authors: Bettina Hünteler; Diego Alburez-Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Much existing research in the demography of kinship focuses on quantifying the number and characteristics of living kin, such as age and sex. We know less about which intergenerational family structures individuals experience throughout their life – for example, when and how long they are parents, children or experience overlap of multiple family generations – although this is important because such trajectories are heterogeneous, potentially producing inequalities in kinship availability across the life. We use simulated micro-level data to project generational placement trajectories for life courses of the complete population of Norway born 1960 and 2000. Our microsimulations use age-specific fertility and mortality rates from 1846 to 2100. First, we benchmark projected trajectories for the 1960 cohort against observed trajectories from empirical register data from 1960 to 2019. Second, we project full life-course trajectories, from age 0 to 100, for the 1960 and 2000 cohorts. Results from sequence analysis show that generational placement trajectories efficiently capture individual-level heterogeneity in intergen-erational kin availability and that results based on our simulated populations largely match those from empirical data. Over cohorts, typical generational placement trajectories will likely become more stable but “thinner”, with later (and shorter) demographic “(double) sandwiching” and increasingly frequent “fading family lines.” The analysis paves the path toward results on a global level and including projections for the future.

articles.title: The Weight of Precedent: Parties, Institutions, and Executive Norms
articles.authors: Daniel A. N. Goldstein; Collin Thomas Schumock
articles.abstract: Political executives often adhere to informal traditions established by their predecessors. Yet, without legal backing, elites have incentives to violate norms for political gain. Under what conditions do constraining executive norms persist and when are they abandoned? We address this question by using an infinite horizon formal model to analyze the maintenance of executive norms. We identify intra-party accountability and variation in patience among actors within the same party as significant for norm maintenance. We also detail how expectations about the expected behavior of out-of-power parties shape the willingness to violate norms while in office. The insights from the model enable us to classify a number of executive norms according to their fragility and to examine the trajectory of one norm in-depth: the two-term tradition of the American presidency. Our findings shed light on how informal institutions regulate executive behavior and advance our understanding of institutional stability and erosion.

articles.title: Indirect Influence: How Elite Attacks on Information Providers Affect Public Opinion Formation
articles.authors: Erik Peterson; Allison Michelle Nam Archer; Kishan Bhakta; SHO IZUMISAWA
articles.abstract: Attacks from politicians can dramatically reduce public trust in sources of expertise and information. We consider the consequences of such criticism and argue that by shaping which information providers their supporters consider credible, politicians can exert indirect influence over public opinion formation. In two survey experiments that link elite criticism of the media to other outcomes, we show politicians who discredit a media outlet cause their supporters to avoid the targeted news source and perceive more bias in its coverage. Partisan attacks also reduce the subsequent effect of the news source's coverage on public opinion, although people are unable to fully discount information from sources they deem untrustworthy due to this rhetoric. Looking beyond direct means of elite influence such as positional cues and policy arguments, we show how harming the reputations of information providers allows politicians to indirectly influence the views of their supporters.

articles.title: Mandatory AI Disclosure Sorts Products into Launch Failure: Evidence from Steam
articles.authors: Kenny Ching
articles.abstract: Platforms increasingly require firms to disclose when products incorporate generative artificial intelligence (AI). Existing evidence largely asks whether such disclosure changes consumer demand; we show that a complementary question—where demand is lost—is at least as important. Using a cross-section of 799 visual-novel games on Steam released early enough to observe a complete 90-day post-release window—of which 22% carry a platform-mandated AI-use disclosure—we show that the consumer response to AI disclosure is concentrated almost entirely on the extensive margin. Disclosed games are roughly twice as likely to obtain no early traction at all: the rate of zero day-30 reviews rises from 5.0% to 9.0%, an odds ratio of 2.14. Among games that do gain an audience, by contrast, the rate of subsequent review accumulation is statistically indistinguishable by disclosure status, and the continuous accumulation penalty is not robust to controls. Disclosed games that are reviewed receive ratings about six percentage points lower. The market response to disclosure is therefore not a uniform discount applied to every product, but a bimodal pattern: a higher probability of failing to launch, and modestly lower satisfaction among survivors. We discuss implications for the design of mandatory disclosure more broadly: when a label can determine whether a product is seen at all, the welfare consequences of disclosure differ sharply depending on whether it gently discounts demand or sorts products into launch failure, and on the producer incentives it sets in motion.

articles.title: SCIENTIFIC FACTS AS CIVILISATIONAL ACHIEVEMENTS: AN ASSESSMENT
articles.authors: Muhammad Abdul Khudus
articles.abstract: Are scientific facts civilisational achievements? Answering this requires clarifying both terms. Drawing on the classical Islamic tradition, namely, al-Fārābī’s virtuous city and the later frameworks of Ibn Khaldūn, Osman Bakar, Wan Mohd Nor Wan Daud, and al-Attas, we argue that a genuine civilisational achievement must engage the physical, mental, and spiritual dimensions of human flourishing, and, on al-Attas’s view, must stand in some relation to revealed Truth. We then characterise a “scientific fact” not as plain truth but as a proposition that is provisionally true: empirically constrained, communally validated, and open to revision. Using three “outdated facts” Pluto’s demotion, the abandonment of the luminiferous aether, and the discovery of additional states of matter, we show that scientific facts are revisable in structurally different ways: definitional, ontological, and enumerative. The deepest layer, the constituent framework or worldview, is never delivered by experiment; it is inherited from the civilisation that produces the science. Every scientific fact is therefore a civilisational achievement, requiring the madīnah, the ummah of inquirers, and a budaya ilmu. But when scientific claims overstep their evidential station and smuggle in an inherited metaphysics, the Muslim community is under no obligation to receive that metaphysics as fact. This, I suggest, is the real meaning of al-Attas’s de-westernization of knowledge: to accept what the instruments have honestly read from the book of creation, while declining the unexamined worldview wrapped around it.

articles.title: Psychological features of dispute content and public acceptance of AI in legal adjudication: evidence for systematic variation beyond individual differences
articles.authors: Masahiro Fujita; Eiichiro Watamura
articles.abstract: Public acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) in legal decision-making has been primarily explained through individual differences in personality traits and general attitudes toward technology. However, emerging evidence suggests that contextual features of legal disputes themselves may systematically influence preferences for AI versus human adjudicators. Across two studies with Japanese participants (N = 1,384 and N = 596), we examined whether psychological characteristics of dispute content—beyond demographics and individual traits—shape acceptability judgments for algorithmic adjudication. Study 1 employed exploratory factor analysis on acceptability ratings across 46 legal dispute vignettes, revealing a robust two-dimensional structure distinguishing interpersonal-relational disputes (where human adjudicators were strongly preferred) from institutional-procedural disputes (where AI acceptance was comparatively higher, though not surpassing human preference in most cases). Study 2 replicated this dimensional structure in an independent sample and demonstrated that experimentally manipulated contextual features—emotional involvement and prototypicality—systematically modulated acceptability judgments, with effects varying by dispositional trust, AI-specific attitudes, and gender. AI-specific expectations emerged as the strongest predictor of acceptance (η2 = 0.252), and a three-way interaction among emotional involvement, gender, and prototypicality indicated that contextual effects are moderated by individual characteristics. These findings suggest that the psychological features of dispute content constitute an overlooked dimension in AI acceptance research, extending beyond technology acceptance models to fundamental questions about how individuals construe social problems and allocate adjudicative authority. We discuss limitations related to measurement approaches, alternative psychological mechanisms, and directions for future research employing real-world case materials and direct assessment of cognitive processes.

articles.title: High resolution measures of preference-based local segregation for the United States, 2018-2023
articles.authors: Jiwon Jang; Dylan Shane Connor; Peter Rogerson; Daoqin Tong
articles.abstract: Neighborhood segregation is a strong driver of disparities in human well-being, yet traditional measures largely ignore the segregation experienced beyond residential neighborhoods. Recent human mobility-based measures have advanced this field by quantifying segregated mobility patterns when choosing travel destinations, but they are often confounded by spatial exposure (i.e., the demographic diversity of the neighborhoods locally reachable from one’s residence) rather than a behavioral preference for similarity. Without adjusting for this baseline exposure, such metrics largely act as proxies for the local residential environment, conflating limited demographic diversity in surrounding areas with active travel decisions to neighborhoods similar to one’s own. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Community Connectivity (CO-CONNECT) dataset, combining billions of anonymized cellphone location records with census tract-level socio-demographic attributes (2018-2023). The dataset operationalizes the Spatial Preference in Local Interaction (SPLIT) index, a local measure of segregation that quantifies the extent to which residents travel to socio-demographically similar neighborhoods, adjusted for the demographic similarity of surrounding neighborhoods. This framework explicitly separates travel decisions that exacerbate group-based segregation from segregation attributable to demographic composition alone, providing a high-resolution picture of mobility-based segregation and its temporal trends across the United States.
